speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext:
That on Monday, October 17th instant, and every Monday thereafter to the end of the session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.
He said: In moving this order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to take the opportunity to express what I believe to be the feeling of most members of this house, namely, appreciation of the interesting debates we have had so far this session on private members' notices of motions and public bills. More time for these debates was made available by the fact that we disposed of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne in much less time than it has occupied in any other session since I first came to this house. Several hon. members have indicated to me that in their opinion the debates on these motions were much more interesting than a protracted debate on the address would have been. Personally I should be inclined to agree with that view. I suggest to hon. members that they think the matter over and ask themselves whether it would be a more interesting use of the time at the disposal of the house to have at the beginning of the session these opportunities for debating the various subjects dealt with in the notices of motions placed on the order paper by private members. I am sure that the debates we have had so far have been interesting and valuable, and I should like to extend my compliments to those who have participated in them.
Several days have been devoted during this session to private members' motions. As hon. members know, there is a large volume of
public business that must be dealt with. Even though we have devoted several days to the consideration of estimates we have not yet disposed of one department in its entirety. It has been found also that discussion of the estimates gives hon. members an opportunity to bring before the house matters which they feel are deserving of consideration, and that it would be well to be able to proceed with the estimates in a more leisurely fashion than is possible at the very end of a session. For this reason I hope that the motion will commend itself to the house, and that, before the business of the session can be considered as completed, ample opportunity will be given to hon. members to deal with matters which appear to them to be of public interest.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS
speechtext: I think that hon. members will agree with much that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said. There is one matter that I should like to mention, Mr. Speaker. On previous occasions the government has first settled upon two or three departments only, and often the estimates of many departments are left until the closing days of the session. The item of departmental administration gives hon. members an opportunity of discussing in a general way the policies and details of the department concerned. I suggest to the government that in this session, and in future sessions, if it meets with their convenience-I am sure it will meet with the convenience of hon. members generally-we have a wider distribution of departments, from the point of view of the estimates presented so that at least the item of departmental administration may be discussed in leisurely fashion. This would meet the wishes of many hon. members who desire not to be rushed at the very last minute in discussing major items. I should like the Prime Minister to take this suggestion into consideration, if he will. It would improve the whole standard of debate.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution was on the order paper at the last session of parliament, but was not reached; consequently we are proceeding with it again at this session.
Hon. members will recall that we have as chapter 78 of the Revised Statutes of Canada an act known as the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act. In 1930 the National Parks Act was passed. It dealt entirely with the national parks and removed from the original bill all the provisions referring to them. In the same year, 1930, the natural resources owned by the dominion in the western provinces were transferred to those provinces, with the result that all national forests which had formerly been set aside were placed under provincial jurisdiction. As a result, the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act, as it exists, is out of date and no longer adequately meets the program and policy of the government.
While it is true that the natural resources of Canada come under provincial jurisdiction, the dominion government does of course recognize that it has a direct interest and responsibility in assisting in the development, protection and utilization of our forest products. The dominion government secures considerable revenue from forest industries. The employment they provide and the subsidiary industries that are maintained have

Canada Forestry Act
contributed in great measure to maintaining the high standard of living which we have at present in Canada. It is not the intention in any way through this bill to invade provincial jurisdiction, but it is felt that by close co-operation and agreement with the provinces we can assist in the development of a constructive forestry program throughout the country. This bill is intended to provide a basis for that assistance.
It should not be assumed that up to the present time nothing has been done in this regard. I would draw the attention of hon. members to some of the activities of the forestry branch. In the dominion forestry service we are at the present time operating three research laboratories, one at Ottawa and one at Vancouver; and we assist in the operation of the pulp and paper research institute at Montreal. The functions of these laboratories are to experiment with new uses of various products, to take steps to preserve the life of the woods we produce, and to prevent waste. In addition to laboratories we have five forest experimental stations which are operating in five different provinces. Those have been set up for the study of problems concerning silviculture, the protection of forests, and the utilization of the products of our forests. Those forest experimental stations cover an area aggregating 227 square miles.
In addition to those laboratories and forest experimental stations we are doing a considerable amount of research work along other lines. For example, we have gathered together a tremendous amount of statistical information that is of great benefit both to the forest industry and to the provinces. By means of air photographs we have been able to secure valuable information as to the extent and quality of the forest resources of this country. New techniques and equipment have been developed which have greatly improved the work being done. The time and the cost required to secure this information have been cut down. I think we might well be gratified to know that the equipment we have developed in this country is now being used in many other countries, as well as by the provincial authorities.
There are many problems concerning forest conservation which require consideration. There is the problem of protecting our forests from fire, from insects, and from disease. These problems are common to all the provinces and undoubtedly can best be met by a combination of effort in research work which will be of benefit to us all.
The problems of reforestation and publicity can best be met by a joint program to be carried out in close co-operation with the provinces. The bill that is to be introduced
(Mr. Gibson (Hamilton West).]
will provide that the dominion government may enter into agreements with the provinces, with other departments of government and with other persons, in order to promote efficient forestry development.
I should like to point out one mistake that has been made in printing the resolution as it appears on the order paper today. This may have been copied from a similar resolution that was up for consideration last session. The resolution reads in part:
The Minister ot Mines and Resources is authorized to appoint temporary officers and employees for the carrying out of the provisions of the act.
There is nothing in the bill giving that authority to the minister, and I do not think it should be in the resolution. Any employees that will be taken on for the purposes of carrying out the activities authorized by the bill will be appointed in the usual way through the civil service.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think we all realize that the conservation and maintenance of our forests is of vital interest to the Canadian people. As a member representing a constituency in which a large number of people derive their livelihood from the forest industry, and as one who has spent almost his whole life in developing a small forest, and in the growing of trees, I take great pleasure in making a few remarks on this resolution.
First of all may I say that I am pleased that the government has decided to introduce this resolution. I shall look forward with interest to seeing the bill that is to follow. The subject of the resolution is of particular interest to me, if you will pardon a personal
Canada Forestry Act
reference, because I am a man who derives far more pleasure from skidding trails, a deck of logs, the perfume of sawn lumber, and woodland operations generally, than from listening to nebulous arguments on some intangible point of law. These things mean more to me and exemplify reality, shall I say.
I am happy to note that in recent years interest in forest conservation has widened. I have made a considerable study of forest conservation, tree planting, selective logging and things of that kind, and looking back over the years I find that there is now a much wider interest in forest conservation and maintenance than there was twenty-five or thirty years ago. I am pleased to note that in recent years trade union organizations and farm organizations in Canada and the United States have expressed themselves as being greatly concerned about the conservation of our timber resources. These people are becoming more aware of the importance of our forests from the point of view of climate, employment, irrigation, and flood control.
Forestry was the first industry on the North American continent. It has been in existence ever since Leif Ericsson came to the shores of this continent and took cargoes of timber back to Greenland. Then there was the development of the lumber industry by the New England colonists who first cut spars for masts for British ships and for shipment to Great Britain. We of this continent are the most fortunate people in the world in having forests containing between 1,100 and 1,200 different species. Today we can see the difference in type between the pulp timber of northern Ontario and the giant trees found in California in the Sequoia national forest, one of which is estimated to contain, if scaled, some 621,000 feet of lumber. Interest in forest conservation in Canada, so far as my reading of the subject is concerned, developed towards the concluding days of the nineteenth century, but the first large-scale organized expression of growing public opinion with respect to the conservation of forests was in the calling of the Canadian forest congress in 1906 by the forestry association of Canada. I believe that congress was called as a result of the successful holding of a similar congress in the United States about twelve months previously.
Although we have had but one major congress in Canada, since that time there has been increasing interest on the part of provincial governments because of their acquiring natural resources within the provinces. At the same time we have had federal government officials doing all they could with the money they had to spend. I should like

Canada Forestry Act
to bring to the attention of the house a paragraph from a pamphlet known as "Forest Facts", published in the 1920's, to indicate how little had been done up to that time. The quotation reads:
The forest resources of Canada are being depleted at the rate of about five billion cubic feet annually through cutting, fire, insects, and decay. If the reproduction and young timber are not protected, the stand of merchantable timber accessible for exploitation will not withstand this drain for more than twenty-five years . . . Few people realize the urgent need which exists for a forest policy in Canada.
That was the situation in the 1920's. We have had the dominion forest conservation commission, which conducted a survey of our forest resources in 1913 and 1914 without making recommendations. As I said before, we have had officials of various departments of the federal government doing limited work in connection with forestry. We have had the provincial governments taking an increasing interest. In addition to these efforts, a very encouraging development in recent years has been the increasing interest of the industry itself. I think it is only fair to say that the forest operators of Canada, large and small, are contributing large sums of money, either toward conservation policies given effect to by individuals, or in support of policies advocated by organizations, and for general publicity purposes to stimulate public awareness of this most important and vital situation.
In this respect I might say in passing that the Canadian Forestry Association has carried on an excellent work throughout the years. Various newspapers, and other publications such as "Woodland World," have also made a contribution. As a result of the fact that we have gradually moved from a pioneer civilization into an industrial civilization, there is a greatly increased consciousness of how basic the forest industry is to Canada. I have read a great deal about various conservation and management policies, and so on. I have read a lot of things written by people who read books and then wrote articles based on pure theory. I have heard lumber operators sometimes unjustly criticized because the person who criticized them did not have knowledge of the conditions under which they were working.
To formulate a policy for forest conservation and for forest management means that you have to formulate a policy to meet a great number of different conditions throughout the country. For instance, on the Pacific coast we have large timber stands with virgin timber that in many cases is five to six hundred years old. It is easy to criticize the operators for cutting those large stands, but on the Pacific coast you must cut virgin and
[Mr. Herridge.l
mature stands clean, and follow with a policy of replanting or of leaving seed trees to carry on reproduction.
In the interior of British Columbia there is an entirely different situation facing operators. They are operating largely in second growth stands with timber up to 125 years old. There they can log selectively. There some operators are beginning to take a limited amount of timber per acre per year from their holdings. Then we come to the timber forest conservation policy of the prairies, where it is almost entirely a policy of replanting under entirely different climatic conditions. Then we come to the pulpwood industry of northern Ontario, which represents an entirely different problem. Therefore in Canada we must have a policy drafted to meet different conditions and changing circumstances. I would urge that the dominion government give every support to the forestry congress proposed by the Canadian Forestry Association to be held in 1950. We all recognize that the management of forests comes directly under the provincial governments, but I am of the opinion that if we are to have an understanding of our forest problems, and if we are to get satisfactory public support for conservation policies that are drafted with a realization of the varying conditions in Canada, we must bring together all interested people at a national congress to function as a clearing house of ideas and opinions. Therefore I urge the minister and his department to give every support possible to the plans for a proposed forestry congress in 1950.
In this connection I should like to quote from an excellent brochure published by the Canadian Forestry Association. I believe it is worth any member's time to read this pamphlet. The excerpt reads:
The Canadian Forestry Association feels it is urgent to the welfare of Canada that a second Canadian forestry congress be convened, with the widest representation from all who are directly and indirectly interested in the forests of Canada.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the essential steps that must be taken to establish a sound forest policy have been well defined as a result of wide Canadian experience. I want to mention briefly some general principles concerning the establishment of such a policy in this country.
In the first place I think we must proceed to halt and control the major destructive forces and processes such as shifting cultivation, overgrazing and burning, and the exploitative and excessive rate of utilization of productive forests. I believe we must create a body of public opinion on forest policy and law, and apply it. through a

competent professional organization. I believe also that we must ensure understanding of and support for these programs; that we must estimate the prospective need for forests in the various provinces, and determine what the forest lands of the country can produce under proper management. I believe it is necessary to apply forestry practices which will be effective and economically feasible, and also to learn a great deal more about forests, forest products and the utilization of waste than is known at present.
I could go on at greater length, Mr. Chairman, but when the bill is introduced I intend to deal with some matters I shall not mention at this stage. I do believe, however, this resolution is evidence that the government is cognizant of greater public interest in the conservation of our forests, and that it now realizes that our forests are a basic resource and must be treated as a national trust. Truly our woods and forests are one in our lives with soil, water, animals and food. Soil and water conservation, flood control, lasting abundance in industry and prosperity on the land-all are involved in the proper use of our forest resources. With all the ravages of the past, the errors and delays, the time required to develop a widespread realization of the problem before us, I am certain that the genius of Canadian democracy can yet restore our forests, redeem our watersheds, bring new life to ghost towns, and find increasingly successful ways to fight fire and pests, if this parliament and the legislatures of this country are willing to give the lead by co-operating one with another.

speechtext: I should like to expand my reply to the question of the hon. member for Nanaimo concerning forests on Indian lands, to point out that while this measure will not directly apply to forest resources on Indian lands, it will of course apply to forest reserves that may be established on those lands.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
I have in mind two questions I should like to ask the minister, but before doing so I want to say briefly how much we appreciate the action of the government in bringing down the legislation which is to be based on this resolution. It must give great satisfaction to Canadians from one end of the country to the other who know anything about the situation that has developed with respect to our forest regions. When we consider the figures which were put on Hansard the other day, showing that in the period from 1940 to 1948 something like 17,000,000 acres of timber land in this country were ravaged by Are; when we realize the tremendous value of the merchantable timber on those lands that were burned over, and when we realize how destructive these fires
Canada Forestry Act
have been, not only to our timber resources but also to our soil and water conservation measures, I believe we must all acknowledge that the minister and the government are to be highly commended on bringing in legislation to provide for closer co-operation with the provinces in better methods of control and utilization of our forest resources.
My constituency of Peace River-not Cariboo, by the way, which is represented by another hon. member-is a big lumber producing area; but year after year we are finding it necessary to go further and further back into uneconomic areas in order to get the timber required. Unless new methods are adopted that will enable forest areas closer to the settlements to produce the lumber which is required, some day it may become economically impossible for our people to get out that timber and make use of it. All too frequently the government of my province has found itself utterly incapable of coping with the fire situation. It just has not the resources. That was one reason why some years ago the province entered into negotiations with the federal government and the predecessors of my hon. friend in the Department of Mines and Resources, with a view to bringing about closer co-operation between the dominion and the provinces with the ultimate objective of preserving the watershed on the east slope of the rockies. Eventually those negotiations bore fruit, and some two years ago a joint board or commission was set up. I understand the work that has been done by that board in the past year and a half has been especially good, and I hope that in the course of his remarks the minister will say something about that work. It seems to me that the joint board set up for the preservation and reforestation of the east slope of the rockies might be a pattern for the action envisioned in this resolution. I would ask the minister, when he has a moment to speak, to give us some report of what has been done and the success that has attended the efforts of that board.

I know that right here in this house we plugged for something to be done with regard to the bud worm; I believe it was with the Minister of Agriculture and also with the Minister of Mines and Resources. In my district this year we had a worm that some people call the army worm. We had it last year too. I believe the province call it the tent caterpillar. It was certainly on the march. They travel as close together as my fingers and travel at such a rate that they could cross the road nearly as fast as a turtle. They just jammed the highways. speechtext:
This resolution deals with the whole ecology of our forests. The forest, whether it is provincial or federal, is like the king, indivisible. Likewise, the impact on the whole forest economy is a total impact on the economy of all of Canada, which cannot be overestimated. For that reason the bill, founded on this resolution, will be welcomed by all sides of the house. So far the debate has done one thing. A large number of members have spoken and they have each posed a different question. In many ways the questions were technical, dealing with reforestation, cutting, pest control, fire and its effect on the water resources of the country.
I want to make a suggestion to the minister. It arises out of the debate we have had this afternoon. In many ways this is a highly technical question. It is not a question on which there can be any political difference of opinion. Every hon. member is as jealous of the forest resources of Canada as any other hon. member; therefore I do hope that when the bill gets into the committee stage the minister will allow it to go to the committee on mines, forests and waters. I make this suggestion specifically so that in the committee we can hear the expert opinion of the pulp and paper industry, the conservation authorities, the provincial forestry authorities, the large timber operators on the Pacific coast, and people such as the wildlife conservationists. All these authorities and all these people have a vital interest in the forests. They all have a special problem. If I may say so, their problems in the main are technical. It would be a great advantage and help to the house if that evidence could be adduced in the committee. It would be a great service to the country to have 
evidence given by experts in that committee. For instance, we could have information on a comparison between Canadian and Scandinavian practices with regard to conservation, cutting and reforestation.
The matter of the water table destruction is important, that is, the ever decreasing and ever deepening level at which water is found practically all over the country. Co-operation with the new river valley authorities set up by the province of Ontario is important. That is a new act passed by the Ontario provincial authorities setting up what are known as river conservation authorities. They take one complete river and plan the conservation of it. Methods and remedies such as the replanting of trees, contour plowing, construction of storage dams and the restoration of the normal flow on the river are used. The most glaring example, and one on which much work has been done in this connection, is the Ganaraska river and now the Thames river near London in western Ontario. As a matter of fact, a very active conservation department is in operation under the Ontario provincial government at the present time.
There is the question of soil erosion and of the value of farmer's woodlot. Then there is the old forest reserves and national parks act. Will it be repealed? Certainly, in many ways, it needs amendment apart altogether from the bill which is to be founded on the resolution we are now discussing.
Then we come to the question whether it is advisable to set up a forest products laboratory such as the forest products laboratory in Madison, Wisconsin, where a great deal of study and research is being done on the use of all kinds of wood products, for example, the use and the salvage of what were waste products such as sawdust and bark, and other waste products which used to be burned. There is the question whether it is feasible to set up such a laboratory in Canada so that the efficiency and economy of the whole wood products industry may be improved. While I understand that stumpage, and dues paid by owners of timber limits, are provincial matters, it would be interesting to know how far that money would go to rehabilitate the land and to replant the forests so that the crops of trees might be continuous, and the land might not be exploited. The forest is a continuous asset; it must not be used as a rich resource to be exploited by the first man or company on the scene.
The restoration of the forest covering in the old and settled parts of Canada is one of the most important matters with

which we could deal. Soil erosion and the resultant destruction of wildlife, the increasing incidence of fires, the destruction of rivers, and the fact that the percentage of farm lands under forest covering has been greatly decreased, far below the limits of safety, are indications of the perils and problems which beset large areas of Canada.
I refer to the importance of forests, not only to the great forest areas of British Columbia and northern Ontario and Quebec, where the forest product industries are located, but more particularly to the importance of forests to farmers and others in the central and southern parts of Ontario and southern Quebec.
These may be technical matters, but there are people in Canada who have the answers. Parliament would be rendering a service if, for these reasons alone, this bill were sent to the committee on mines, forests and waters, so that every hon. member and the people throughout the country may have explicit, accurate and complete information on the vital problem of preserving our Canadian forests.

I mention this only because a few moments ago the Prime Minister, answering a question with respect to the introduction of housing legislation at an early date, indicated that one of the reasons the measure had not been proceeded with earlier was that he did not want the provinces to learn for the first time some aspects of the dominion government's point of view in any legislation which might be brought down. He indicated, in other words, that he was anxious that the provinces should have a fair opportunity to discuss the whole matter before legislation was brought to the house.
In expressing agreement with the principle of the resolution, I wish to have it understood that I believe it is important that in all matters such as this, where it is the intention of the dominion government to co-operate with provincial jurisdictions, the dominion should be very careful to lay the groundwork well in the first instance, so that there may be no reason for a lack of co-operation at a later time.
Canada Forestry Act
I have no doubt our forests are assets which present a challenge to the minds of every member in the house and of our people generally. I remember in my earlier years attending a public meeting in Ontario and hearing the late Hon. William Finlayson, the then provincial minister of lands and forests, deliver a speech. I believe that would be some time in the twenties. In that speech he referred to our forests as a crop and said -and I agree with him-that too often we have regarded our forests as a necessarily wasting asset instead of handling them as we would ordinary field crops. He pointed out that we would not think of planting a grain crop in the agricultural areas, and then proceed to harvest them without doing something about the next crop. He added that in some instances it took more than fifty years for those crops to develop.
I remember clearly the response to that suggestion by an old gentleman from a farming district in the county of Peel. This old gentleman, whom I knew well, sat in the front seat of the meeting. I hesitate, in the presence of such a highly developed and sensitive group of gentlemen, to use his expression; but the old gentleman said, "Mr. Minister, did you say fifty years?" and when Mr. Finlayson said that he had, the old gentleman said, "Well, to a farmer like myself that seems to me like a damned slow crop".
I believe that the pioneering work done at that time did create in the minds of the people generally the thought that, after all, the forests must be regarded as a crop, in the ordinary sense of the term. If I were to offer any criticism of the resolution it would be that perhaps we had begun too late to deal with this great asset, this important heritage.
I was looking up a few figures a short time ago and, while I have not all of them up to date, the ones I have indicate that we have in Canada three-quarters of a million square miles of productive forest lands. That, in itself, constitutes a challenge in the matter of conservation. It has been pointed out that ninety per cent of the forest areas in Canada are owned by the crown either in the right of the province or in the right of the dominion. I have no doubt the minister will agree that that means that a move of this kind is made that much easier by virtue of the nature of the ownership of those forests.
Figures show that in the past the dominion government has spent less than half of one per cent of the revenues derived directly or indirectly from the lumbering industry on the conservation of our forests, and general expenditures in relation thereto. When one

realizes that out of every 100,000 feet of lumber cut an additional 40,000 is lost through fire, insects anu disease he must have some understanding of the importance of any measure which, working co-operatively between the dominion and the provinces, will bring to an end at least some of the wastage so apparent in this great national heritage and asset.
In our section of Canada, as the hon. member for York West pointed out a few moments ago, a section which has been settled for perhaps a longer period of time than some others, the questions of soil conservation, flood damage and flood control have been engaging the attention of our provincial authorities.
I never could see eye to eye with the dominion government-of course this is not the first time-in its policy toward the river authorities which were set up to deal with the Thames, the Ganaraska, the Etobicoke and other rivers. I have often wondered why they did not take advantage of the opportunity afforded by the provincial legislation to bear part of the expense of operating those projects. The provincial legislation which was passed about two years or more ago provided that the municipalities immediately involved would pay 25 per cent of the cost, the provincial government 37J per cent and the dominion government 37J per cent. Perhaps the minister is unaware of the long negotiations that took place because the representations were not made to his department, but the dominion government declined to pay anything toward the cost of operating the various authorities set up. The result has been that the provincial government has had to bear 75 per cent of the cost of the works that were undertaken, while the municipalities have paid for the balance.
I am glad to see that there is an indication that the dominion government has become conscious of the necessity of working hand in hand with the provinces in a great and forward-looking venture for the purpose of preserving this most important, although slowly developing crop, and seeing that in the days that lie ahead we shall not have wasted this great heritage that is ours.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that one of the greatest menaces to our forests-I am referring now to my own province and county-is the operators themselves. It has been asked whether this legislation will invade provincial jurisdiction. In New Brunswick our forests have been mismanaged and today it is necessary that the federal government come to our assistance.

In my own county the method of logging 25 years ago could be styled as a horse-and-buggy method. If we had to depend upon that same method today our mills would be closed because it is now necessary to haul logs as far as 100 to 150 miles in order to get supplies to the mills. The land in the immediate vicinity of the mills has been cut and slashed and the result is that nothing is left. I am referring now to crown and privately owned lands in my county.
I have walked through tracts of land in the county of Charlotte and have noted how they were crisscrossed with roads that had been dug with bulldozers through the woods. To my way of thinking that was hardly necessary. It will take at least 50 years or possibly 100 years before anything worth while can be grown on that land. I know of one particularly nice stand of spruce in my county that was sold two years ago for stumpage. I know quite well the gentleman who cut that off. He was instructed to cut everything that would make a two by three. The result was that what had been a fine piece of woodland was nothing but waste and would be nothing but waste for another 50 years.
I believe in free enterprise; but my thought is that, though you may give all the assistance you wish to the provinces, until there is some form of forest management in the provinces it will be a waste of time and good money. History shows that those European countries which have had planned forest management have forests that are more valuable today than they were thirty or forty years ago, but you cannot find that situation in New Brunswick.
The large companies have gone in and cut and slashed and destroyed without any thought of future generations. If the federal government feel that they are in position to help the provinces there should be some method evolved whereby this destruction will be made impossible in future. We now have members in the house from Newfoundland, a province which is sometimes referred to as backward. However, from the information I am able to gather, they have a much better system of forest management than exists in any of the provinces of Canada. They are protecting their forests.
It might be said that when the government steps in and tells you that you must not touch this or that in the forest we would be getting away from freedom of action, but I think this industry has been brought to a position where some means must be found to protect it if it is to be carried on in the future.
I would think that the people who would be more interested than any others in the

preservation of our forests would be the operators themselves. If they would agree to some plan for the preservation of our forests, I think they might be in position to ask for federal assistance. If assistance is going to be given and the operators still allowed to cut and slash and destroy as they wish, it will give those citizens who are providing the funds for this purpose little encouragement to support such a subsidy.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see that the hon. member for Quebec South is in his seat. I know that he is better qualified to speak on this subject than I, but I am going to say a few words and I know that as he is a good friend and citizen he will not make any remarks. I am not an expert on this matter but I do want to take part in this debate, speaking only as a citizen who is anxious to see developed a general offensive which may result in a victorious battle against fire, insects, wastage and perhaps apathy in some quarters, the result of which is destroying slowly but surely one of our greatest assets.
My remarks will be confined entirely to personal observations. Not being an expert, as I have said, in order to sustain my contention I shall have to rely upon what has been said by those whose goal it is to preserve our forests against devastation by the means to which I have just referred.
Many people who are members of protective associations, forestry associations, the Canadian pulp and paper industry and so on are constantly looking for new designs and methods which may be used to develop a program which could be studied and perhaps finally accepted by the various provincial governments. Concerted action may be the successful means of giving the assurance of a new era in the protection of our trees, the continuance of our water power and, to a certain extent, the permanent irrigation of our soil. Some have proposed that a national congress should be held, but I suggest that there should be a dominion-provincial conference to deal with this matter and study it carefully. The apathy of our population may prove disastrous if even the layman is not interested and leaves the job to be done by others.
I often have the privilege of enjoying fishing and hunting trips in the Laurentides. My county is divided into two parts from east to west by the Laurentides, these lovely and enchanting mountains, the oldest in the country. I have often noticed the lack of cautiousness shown by some people in the handling of camp fires, matches and so forth. We will never know the loss suffered by the
45781-m
Canada Forestry Act
taxpayers of Canada because of carelessness and lack of proper education. People should at least be willing to observe the warning posted in that forest. They only have to read the posters issued by the different associations and governments by the thousand and meditate on the meaning of one sentence that can be read on them, namely:
One tree can produce one million matches; one match can destroy one million trees.
But how many read it, and if they do so how many think of it and for how long?
The trouble lies in the absence of the program of widespread education I was advocating a few moments ago. Preventive medicine has learned that education must start at home with the help of the father and mother so that our children will know where danger lies. Prevention of forest destruction by fire and insects should begin at home and be continued in the primary and secondary schools. Naturally when a child grows older he is inclined to forget, and if public opinion is not aroused it will endanger and probably render impossible what I might call, when I speak of reforestation, the resurrection of the Canadian forest.
The arousing of public opinion is urgent. I hope that the step taken by the Minister of Mines and Resources will strike the right note, show the way, and provide the necessary incentive so that the march towards realization will be on for good. I urge the members of the house to look carefully into the wells of information given to us by the Canadian Forestry Association. Not being an entomologist I will not discuss the loss the forests of Canada have suffered from insects, but I will say a few words about wastage. Walking in the forest I often have deplored the enormous quantity of timber lost by careless exploitation. The forestry association tells us that five hundred million cubic feet are wasted in logging each year, and that you have to add to that figure four hundred million cubic feet wasted in sawmill operations. You will see what that amounts to in the depletion of our forests.
In co-operation with the provinces we should find a way to use waste timber of all dimensions which is left on the ground and provides, if not cleared out, a wonderful centre of culture for insects and fires. In the wintertime many poor people need fuel wood. Even in the best managed country of the world there will always be poor people. My proposal is to form an organization whose function would be to collect this lost timber, haul it out of the forest and forward it to charitable institutions in various communities so that the poor would be provided with

Canada Forestry Act
the fuel wood they lack. With the help of the various governments interested, Canadian Forestry Association contractors, jobbers and others, we might come to a point where it would be possible to work out a system to give, to those in need, fuel wood which otherwise would be left to the ravages of fires and insects. I think I could see from the remarks of the minister that he had in mind the elaboration of a general program of research and education to be carried on co-operatively by the federal and provincial governments.
Let us follow the example of a highly industrialized nation which years ago climbed the ladder of fame by its industry. They left nothing untouched; they created something out of almost nothing and came to a point where an industry was the pivot of world industry. If an insane leader had not misled that nation her potentiality would still be a power to deal with. I refer to the German nation. Let us be industrious and use the waste, reference to which is found in the pamphlet sent to us by the Canadian Forestry Association, and which is entitled "The Case for Forestry in Canada". They show that the waste from fire, insects and disease is eight hundred million cubic feet annually, and they go on to say:
This loss can be greatly reduced by better protection and education.
I stress the reference to education. It should be enlarged and forced into the minds of our people, especially our children. The pamphlet continues:
Waste in utilization.
Logging waste	500 million cubic feet
Sawmill waste	400 million cubic feet
If we were as industrious as the German people we would not lose that waste. We would bring it out somehow by means of some kind of organization. It takes only good will, co-operation, understanding, and an absence of political purposes, to form an organization of that kind so that we can use every piece of that timber that we see in the forests, which is now good for nothing and is lost to the population. It is only good for the insects and for fires. We could use it for the benefit of our population. We all remember that before the war the Germans used to manufacture tin toys for the little ones out of tin cans. We should follow that example, and I am sure that everyone in the country will be satisfied. The children will be glad to know. It would be a lesson in patriotism for them to know that a great deal of our timber is being used for their own benefit. To that end we need an example from the government and these associations.

I hope that the program the minister wants to put into effect will be followed by everyone, and that the march is on for the recovery and resurrection of our Canadian forests.

speechtext:
I wish to support the resolution of the government. There was never a time in the history of Canada when a national forest policy was more needed. We are a nautical people, and it took the second world war to show the country the necessity of conservation of the forests on the part of federal, provincial, municipal and other public bodies. Prior to the second war they were depleted by almost fifty per cent. The historian Parkman devoted several pages of his history book to the forests of our country and the need to preserve them for future generations; but, as I have said, they have been squandered at an alarming rate.
In speaking on this resolution I want to congratulate the Canadian Forestry Association on the good work it has done in this connection. This is one of the most constructive steps to be taken by the government at this or any other session. There never was a time in the history of Canada when we were more in need of a national policy to protect our forests. Parkman referred to the Indians and Eskimos away up in the northland, and said there was not a river entered or a cape turned but the way was led by an Indian or Eskimo. They were with Frobisher, they were with Hudson, they were with Mackenzie, and they were with Fraser when those men explored these great rivers. They helped show the people of southern Canada what a great heritage we have in our forest resources.
This resolution also refers to other matters which I am not going to mention, since I am going to speak only for three or four minutes. It provides that the government will-
-exercise control and management thereof and construct works therein; establish and maintain forest research laboratories; assist provinces or owners of forests and enter into agreements respecting the protection and development of forest lands.
That all links up with what Parkman had to say. The old schoolbooks used in both the public and separate schools of this country contained large pictures having to do with these matters, and the subject now has reached the universities, where I am glad to say they have research and forestry departments. We certainly should teach the rising generation something about the history of their own country, the wealth of vast forest resources, and the influence the forests have on water power, lumbering, logging and forestry.
This resolution also deals more or less with water power. We have a potential of

45,000,000 horsepower in this country, of which only one-seventh has been developed at the present time; and part of that is only seasonal, where some industries require it for only three or four months in the year. The great development in hydroelectric power brought about by the second world war has helped to fulfil the dreams of those who have been associated with this project for many years past and wanted a national hydro policy for Canada.
The history of the timber industry in Canada goes back for many years. Away back in 1885 loggers were taken from the city of Ottawa and other parts of Canada all the way to the Nile river, where they assisted in the relief of General Gordon at Khartoum. We are a nautical people, and Providence has provided us with a magnificent chain of rivers and inland streams and lakes. We are also fortunate in that we have great deposits of some twenty-five or thirty minerals; and for all these reasons we have long needed a national policy of this kind. If you turn to Houston's Annual, which used to be a standard textbook, you will find that much of the wealth of this country, including the timber along great sections of the Ottawa river, has been underwritten by and turned over to interests in New York city. I am glad that now we are going to develop a national policy for the protection of our own natural resources. During the last war, when we were giving minerals, lumber and many other things to Russia, and when we were told that from Puget sound north we had 760 miles of undefended coast, it was suggested that we should have a national policy of conservation. Now I hope that policy will be really developed. I remember when the harbour of Toronto was being developed, and we had to bring very heavy timber and logs all the way down through the Panama canal and up to Toronto for that work; and it was wonderful timber. If any hon. members visited the trade fair held in Toronto last May they must have seen something of the great importance of the timber wealth of our Pacific province to this country. As an example, Douglas fir and many other kinds of lumber are used in about twenty-six different forms in public buildings throughout the east, and in Toronto our public buildings, schools and national exhibition use all these; which shows what can be done by means of conservation.
I am glad to see this resolution on the order paper today. We have needed a national policy for a long time, and I hope now something will be done about it. I think a great deal can be done by means of education. We read of the great fires that occur in our timber lands and the wealth lost as a result; and
Canada Forestry Act
it is appalling to realize how little is being done to preserve our forests for future generations. We have the greatest natural resources of any country on earth. Compared with other countries our forests represent unlimited wealth, together with our copper, zinc, platinum, gold, silver, asbestos, tin and other minerals. I believe the time has come when we should have a national policy not only for our forests but for our mineral resources, so that the wealth of this country may be safeguarded. It belongs to the people of Canada, and I believe that here we have a constructive resolution which will help develop in this country government of the people, by the people and for the people.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
I am glad the government is going to introduce a bill designed to assist in the conservation of our forest resources. During recent years there has been an increasing awareness on the part of the general public, on the part of people engaged in the timber industry and on the part of governments of the necessity for better methods of forest management and improved forest conservation.
I do not intend to go into those matters today, however. I saw something of the forests of Great Britain, Italy and northwestern Europe; and one has only to see those forests to realize that we in Canada have a long way to go to catch up with the countries of Europe in the matter of forest management, conservation, reforestation, and so on.
In his remarks today the minister, as far as I could gather, did not say anything about the first part of this resolution. He spoke chiefly of what this measure was going to do to enable the dominion government to assist the provinces and to work in conjunction with them. However, I am far from clear as to exactly what this bill that is to be introduced is to do. What is the purpose of it? I should particularly like to know what the first part of this resolution means:
That it is expedient to present a bill to authorize the governor in council to establish as a national forest or as a forest experimental area lands belonging to His Majesty in the right of Canada . . .
And so forth. As far as I know, the only lands in the control of the dominion government are those in the Yukon, in the Northwest Territories, in the Indian reserves and in the dominion parks.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext: May I point out to my hon. friend that we have such lands as the Petawawa military area and some on military lands of that type.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
In addition to the areas I have indicated there are, then, the military reserves. However, the minister has already

Canada Forestry Act
pointed out that it is not proposed apparently to establish any of the Indian reserves as national forests or forest experimental areas. I should like the minister to tell us just what the first part of this resolution means. Where are national forests to be established? Is it proposed to establish a national forest in the Northwest Territories, or is it proposed to use part or parts of some of the national parks, such as Banff national park or Jasper national park, for that purpose? When those national forests are established, what is the purpose of them? Are they going to be used as part of a reforestation scheme or as examples, you might say, of what can and should be done in the matter of forest culture? Exactly what is the purpose of them? It seems to me that before the resolution goes through we should have a little bit more information with regard to the matters I have mentioned.

speechtext: Is the minister going to answer?

speechtext:
Several
questions have been asked. I was waiting to hear any other members who were desirous of speaking on the motion. The last speaker has asked what was the purpose of the act. In the first place we are, under the act, repealing an old act that has been on our statute books for a good many years and which dealt not only with national forests but with national parks; and we are bringing the legislation into line with the present program of the government. We also have five experimental stations on which forestry research is being conducted, and experiments are being carried on in the matter of forest conservation. This bill will not override the National Parks Act or the Indian Act, but if it is at any time later deemed advisable to declare some of the dominion lands to be national forests, it gives us power to do so. There is no immediate intention to do so. For example, we have an experimental station on the military area at Petawawa. While that land belongs to the Department of National Defence, through negotiations with that department we maintain an experimental station there.
The hon. member for Peel asked if we had had any previous consultation with the provinces. While I was not in this department at the time, I understand that the appropriate ministers of all the provinces except Prince Edward Island submitted a brief to the government as far back as 1943, asking practically for what is now provided for in this bill. Subsequently the matter was informally discussed with each of the provincial governments, so that they would know what it was

proposed to include in the bill; and I am informed that the majority, if not all, have expressed strong approval of this measure.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
Before I deal with the resolution proper, I want to say that I thoroughly agree with it, but I should like to ask the minister who was the authority from the tenth province that was consulted in 1943. I should not imagine there was such a person. I should be interested in knowing if such were the case.
As to the resolution itself, it entails the presentation of a bill. I cannot imagine anybody opposing the resolution. As I am sure all hon. members must know, forty per cent of all United States dollars earned by Canada come from the Canadian pulp and paper industry. I believe that some one-quarter of a billion dollars is paid out annually in wages in Canada by that industry. Three out of every five newspaper pages printed anywhere in the world are printed on Canadian paper or on paper made from Canadian pulp. If that fact in itself is not sufficient to indicate the importance of the bill which it is proposed to introduce, as indicated by the minister today, I do not know what more hon. members would require. To me this measure is extremely important not only for Canada as a whole but particularly for what one of the hon. members today termed "the backward province of Newfoundland". I may say that we do not regard Newfoundland as being backward, and we shall regard this term as being used in a humorous way.
I might add, however, that the greatest single contribution to the Canadian economy, as a result of confederation, was the pulp and paper industry of Newfoundland. This industry brought into the Canadian economy some $40 million. That is no small amount when it is considered that it came from a province with a population as small as that of Newfoundland, particularly when it is recognized that sixty-five per cent of the newsprint produced in Newfoundland is sold in the United States for United States dollars. It is difficult these days to get away from the Yankee dollar.
In passing I should like to refer to a couple of statements made by the heads of our pulp and paper industries in Newfoundland. I hope it will not be deemed inappropriate, because I want to deal with them a little bit further later on. As a result of devaluation I feel that hon. members should know the views of these important people; at least they are important to us. This is a C.P. dispatch dated September 30, from Corner Brook, and reads as follows:
Sir Eric Bowater, president of Bowater's Pulp and Paper Mills here, biggest in the world-

I may say that the pulp and paper mill at Corner Brook in Newfoundland is the biggest single paper mill of its kind in the world.
-yesterday expressed the hope of obtaining more United States markets for newsprint in view of the expected loss of sale to the United Kingdom.
Sir Eric was commenting on a report from London that Britain proposes to switch her huge newsprint imports from the dollar markets of Canada to soft-currency sources in Scandinavia.
He said his company now is planning to increase production to meet further orders agreed upon for delivery to the United States in January, 1950.
He warned mill workers, however, that costs of production must come down and quality improve if the company were to expand sales in the highly competitive U.S. market. "The U.S. publishers can assure us a market only if the price is right," he said.
On the sulphite pulp situation, the president said markets in the sterling area have already been lost, but it was thought an outlet might be found in the United States.
That is the Corner Brook mill. Here is the Grand Falls picture:
The entire Canadian newsprint industry may be on short time next year, E. M. Little, president of Anglo-Newfoundland Development Company, said yesterday.
The president of the newsprint firm, commenting on a London report that Britain will buy her newsprint in Scandinavia instead of Canada to save dollars, said in a statement:
"The American market is at present good, but if the business decline in the United States continues, newsprint must eventually be affected . . .
The whole of the Canadian industry may be on short time next year, but to what extent is difficult to forecast as yet.
Conditions are not bright but this company must become and continue to be competitive. As money becomes available this mill will be modernized."
The reason I am quoting these statements is that a measure such as the proposed bill will be of great value in bringing down the cost of the production of newsprint. I take it that that is part of the program that the minister would contemplate in the investigation that he proposes to have made by the various research boards to be set up.
I would recommend that hon. members read the September 17 edition of the Financial Post. I believe every hon. member has been provided with a copy. I was. It is of great interest to anybody who is concerned with the pulp and paper industry and the value of that industry to the economy of Canada. One excerpt I should like to read is a statement by Mr. D. W. Ambridge, president of Abitibi Power and Paper Company, which was made to a pulp and paper meeting earlier this year. He was asked a question as to how much should be spent by industry on research if it is to do a proper job. He said that $6,400,000 annually should be spent by industry in research. That is entirely apart from the government assistance. There are five more points to which he referred and I should like
Canada Forestry Act
to read them to the committee. They are as follows: Here he is referring to starting points for research:
Wasted trees-millions of trees die each year from old age or disease or fire. Some are inaccessible, but most should not have perished. Research is needed to develop methods of saving them-new cures, new fire suppression methods, new uses for everything the forest grows instead of only the trees the industry can most easily use.
Waste liquors from chemical processes-usually disposed of, they carry away with them untold quantities of various materials which will some day be used. Sugars in the sulphite liquor are now being utilized in alcohol and yeast manufacture.
Bark-Mountains of bark are lying unused beside mills, yet in Europe bark is a valuable ingredient in a variety of products.
Lumber-Hundreds of small sawmills make lumber out of small logs, often waste 50 per cent of the wood in the tree. Even the finished lumber itself is often wasted; on construction jobs, for instance, where lumber used for concrete forms is usually burned afterward as part of tidying up.
Other fields for research-Development of efficient mechanized equipment for woods operations, including thorough clean-up after well-planned cutting, in order to make use of the slash, leave behind best possible conditions of growth for young trees and seeds. Application of the latest developments in science to the paper-making process. New by-products.
What's being done about these problems. On an industry basis, one of the most important factors in pulp and paper research has been the pulp and paper research institute which is a co-operative venture founded in 1928 by the industry in conjunction with the Canadian government and McGill university.
The minister referred to this institute. In the same article he said that up to 1947 the industry gave $50,000 a year to this research institute, but it is now giving $100,000 a year. When the minister replies will he tell us what the government is contributing to that institute and how much is being paid by industry?
In conclusion I should like to quote from page 52 of the same paper:
Pulp and paper men say that a national forest policy is necessary and that its needs are few and relatively simple.
First, they say, Canada should have complete air surveys and maps of the forests. Today their extent is not even completely known and there is no comprehensive and proper estimate of forest increment in Canada.
Secondly, Canada needs to check the insects and diseases which periodically reach epidemic proportions. Also greater effort is required to prevent the ravages of fire. Lightning is constantly causing fires in crown land forests and forest operators are constantly threatened by fires in unoccupied forest areas adjacent to their limits.
Finally, industry men say that Canada should increase the extent of its research work on the forests and on forest products.
Both federal and provincial authorities have through research contributed to the development of agriculture, minerals, and fisheries, but the forests receive less attention. Pulp and paper men say that the forests require at least as much interest and attention as are given to other valuable national resources.

Canada Forestry Act
That, Mr. Chairman, rather sums up the picture as far as I know it. But the value of our forests is important to the economy of Canada, and its value to the province of Newfoundland is so great that one can do nothing but most heartily endorse the resolution. Since we have problems which are peculiar to our province I should like to ask the minister whether it is not possible to place one of these research bureaux-in fact anything that is envisaged in this resolution 

in the province of Newfoundland. We have nothing in the maritime provinces. We have one in Vancouver and one in Montreal and there is one in Ottawa. Certainly, the mari-times are entitled to one, and naturally the newest province, with all its problems, with all its worries, with the value to it of the forest industry, should be entitled to one of these research bureaux.

speechtext:
After listening to the discussion I have wondered just exactly what the resolution means. As I understand it, the minister has merely moved a resolution for the purpose of introducing a bill. It remains to be seen what that bill will contain. This is not the place for a major speech. I am going to reserve whatever criticism I may have of the bill until it comes up for second reading. I am just wondering what the minister or his advisers had in mind because of the way the resolution is worded. Although a wide discussion has been permitted I cannot see where the resolution has anything to do with the pulp and paper industry. The fact of the matter is I cannot see that it is intended to bring in a bill that means anything if the wording of the resolution means anything. I say this for the minister's benefit. I hope that it is not the intention of the bill to set up a central experimental board for the purpose of providing research facilities for the benefit of those who exploit the forests of this country for profit. If the wording of the resolution means anything, that is my conception of it. It has nothing to do with reforestation; not a word is mentioned about that. It has nothing to do with conservation. It has nothing to do with the pulp and paper industry. So far as I can see, it is the intention merely to provide a small experimental area somewhere for the purpose of spending the government's money to carry on research for the benefit of those who exploit the forests for profit.
I cannot agree with those who take the position that it is a wonderful thing for us to be sending the real wealth of Canada to the United States or to some other country so as to bring in American dollars. Unfortunately that is the position we are in today; that is one of the fallacies of the system. I

believe however the day is coming, and coming pretty fast, when that will be corrected.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext: You cannot eat newsprint.

maintopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
But we can process our pulp in this country, and create an industry here which will pay wages to our workers. Except in Newfoundland, the maritime provinces have very little by way of a pulp and paper industry. I am safe in saying that 80 per cent of the pulpwood from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick crosses the border to be processed in the United States. The wages are paid over there. The product comes back to Canada, and we pay a high price for it. I say it should be processed here.
Dollars are not the real wealth of a country. We send our real wealth out of the country when we export our products. I hope that when the minister brings in his bill the areas he intends to set up as research laboratories will have something to do with fire prevention. I trust there may be some definite recommendation in that connection, because the greatest destroyer of our forests is fire.
Secondly, I hope that if and when this area is developed a part of the research will deal with ways and means of processing our own lumber, building up a pulp and paper industry of our own, putting our own people to work and making proper use of our own resources. If the federal government is to provide funds for that purpose, then I hope the minister will tell us to what extent the pulp and paper industry, or any other industry in Canada which may gain from such research, will be taxed. The operator pays stumpage. If the federal government intends to set up these research facilities, to what extent will the industries contribute to it?
I trust that when the minister brings in the bill he will give on second reading some information as to the mechanics of operation, because I want to have the answers to these questions. That is why I am asking now, so that fire prevention, reforestation and all these other matters may be taken into consideration when this area is being developed.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a forester I am pleased to see the interest taken by hon. members in the legislation, because in my view the proposed measure is an important one. Forest conservation is of major importance to the lumbering industry. I cannot agree with the hon. member for Cape Breton South when he says that in this proposed legislation he sees only the installation of an experimental station; because the resolution states that the government is anxious to

co-operate with the owners and with provincial governments so as to enter into agreements respecting the protection and development of forest lands.
I must say as a forester that in the past I have had occasion to see evidence of the co-operation which has existed between the federal and provincial governments, and the different owners of timber limits and private lands. The measure now before the committee has been prepared because of the encouragement given to the exploitation of the forests in a scientific manner. The measure looks toward the improvement of the management of forest areas for the purpose of conserving and perpetuating the forest empire in Canada, an empire which occupies more than a third of the whole area of our country and stretches from the Atlantic to the Pacific in a belt ranging from 600 to more than 1,200 miles wide.
It is said that the forests are the spinal column of Canada's economy, and they form a great source of wealth for our country. Our forests offer a great attraction to tourists, and a sanctuary for wildlife. The annual wealth produced by our forest industries is tremendous. The annual harvest of forest products, plus the value added by manufacturing, is over a billion dollars-and this figure does not include the transportation of the various products, or the revenues from tourists, hunting or fishing.
One of the most important characteristics of our forests is that they are a product of the soil. Like the farmers' crops, our forests grow; unlike the farmers' crops they take many years before they are ready for harvesting. The science of forestry is based upon the principle of treating the forests as a crop during the growing period, and harvesting that crop in such a way that another will follow.
This is called silviculture-and is the tilling of the forests, just as agriculture is the tilling of the land. The job of the forester is to practise forestry, and to produce from the forests the greatest possible quantities of the most valuable products in the shortest time and at the lowest possible price.
In many parts of the world the only effective way to reproduce forests is by planting, what we call artificial reforestation. Fortunately in our country conditions of soil and temperature help natural reforestation. It is important however that we do more artificial reforestation, especially near unproductive lands located in the vicinity of pulp mills or saw mills. By passing this legislation I think the government will help the provinces and the different owners of timber limits.
Canada Forestry Act (Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to speak at length on this subject. Since my profession is related to the timber industry, howover, I should like to say a few words.
I am sure that in all parts of the country, everyone interested in lumbering is glad to know that the government intends to introduce this legislation now. I would suggest to hon. members that they secure, if possible, a copy of "La Foret quebecoise", especially the July-August and the September, 1948, issues, and read therein the pastoral letter of His Grace Monsignor Labrie, bishop of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. In his letter, Monsignor Labrie stresses the importance of the forest. He points out how we have neglected the forest, the source of one of our largest industries. I wish to quote a few paragraphs from the letter, as published in the July-August, 1948, issue. Speaking of the forest, Monsignor Labrie quotes Professor B. E. Fernow, LL.D.:
"It can be said without fear of contradiction," wrote Professor Fernow, "that next to the products necessary for the sustenance of human life nothing is so widely used, so essential in domestic and public economy as timber. It is impossible to conceive of civilization without lumber, large quantities of lumber." Those words, written in 1906, are still amazingly timely. In spite of staggering development in other spheres of industry, new techniques and uses, as well as transformations of a physical and chemical nature, the lumber industry has maintained its enviable position in the economy of our country.
We must protect our forests. Bishop Labrie, who is an authority in that field, mentions elsewhere in his pastoral letter, some of the steps initiated by various governments. I repeat his words, although I have no intention of praising our governments. Here is what Bishop Labrie writes:
Before setting forth the duties of each and everyone, we wish to commend what has already been done. As early as 1903, Professor B. E. Fernow, LL.D., stirred public interest in the matter by his series of impressive lectures. Since then, government authorities and lumber companies as well as universities, have spent large sums of money for the establishment of schools of forestry. In addition, they have sent engineers, specialized in forestry, to study the organization of the magnificent European forests.
Bishop Labrie, who assuredly held no brief for any government, obviously recognized, however, to what extent various administrations and other organizations had helped the forest industry. I fully appreciate that a great deal remains to be done in this respect, because forests are not only a national asset but also a national problem, one that should

recently by a well known Canadian, Leonard Knott, and like his other books it is exceedingly well done. Leonard Knott is a Canadian who thinks that we have just as much of interest in this country as there is in the United States and he has demonstrated his belief by writing a series of books for children, including "The Children's Book of the Saguenay" and "The Children's Book of the Great Lakes" and now this latest one, "The Children's Book of Trees".

It is addressed particularly to children but is good reading for adults, too. I am sure that these two books would do a good job of interesting the children and young people in our schools in this great natural resource.
The other comment I should like to make has to do with fire prevention. It seems to me we should pursue every suggestion that might help to eliminate the destruction of our forests by fires. My colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, has already referred to the tragic loss by fire that we sustain every year.
In this connection I have been following the efforts that have been made by interested people in the United States and by some people in Canada to ascertain the extent to which cigarettes are the cause of forest fires. I understand there has been on foot for a number of years, particularly in the United States, a move to have eliminated from cigarettes saltpetre or such other chemicals as are put in them for the express purpose of making them burn faster. I do not happen to smoke myself so I cannot speak with too much authority, but I understand cigarettes do not last very long, and that apparently the tobacco people would not be too interested in anything that would make them last longer because then hon. members of the house would not have to buy so many more.

The whole idea which I am suggesting is that if cigarettes could be made in such a way that, when discarded, they would not produce fires so readily we might save ourselves a great deal of the loss that we now sustain. I am told that the matter

has been a subject of interest on the part of people in the United States for twenty or twenty-five years. I am also told that they have not made much headway yet. The interests on the other side-namely the tobacco people-are pretty powerful, but that is no reason for not proceeding at least with research.
Press reports indicated that this question was discussed at the annual convention of the association of Canadian fire marshals held a month or so ago. It was indicated that representations might be made to the federal government asking them to bring in legislation outlawing the manufacture or sale of such cigarettes as I have referred to, which are so ready a fire hazard. I asked certain questions about this matter on the order paper, but the answers I got on October 3 of this year, as found at page 439 of Hansard, were not very helpful. Accordingly I wrote to the office of the dominion fire commissioner and had a very interesting letter in reply in which I was told that, although the representations were not made formally by the association of Canadian fire marshals to the government, nevertheless the president of that association has been making such representations, and has suggested to the government that definite research in this matter be pursued.
I suppose that one of the places for that research to be done is the national research council, but I notice that the resolution now before us calls for research work as to our forests. I suppose that research in the main is towards developing ways and means of increasing growth, methods of reforestation, and so on, but it would seem to me that it would also be a legitimate subject of research to go into the question of the extent to which cigarettes are the cause of forest fires. If it turns out that those who are interested in this matter are right, and that cigarettes with saltpetre in them are a major cause of forest fires, surely it would be the part of wisdom for the government to bring in legislation to improve the situation. I hope the minister will give the same sympathetic consideration to this point that I am sure he will give to my suggestion about getting more copies of that beautiful book of his into the schools of the country.
