speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries) moved
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure for the purpose of regulating the inspection of fish and fish containers and of marine plants for export and import, and to provide for the appointment of inspectors and other officers and employees required for the proper administration of the act.

On the previous measure I asked the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Gibson) if he would not make his statement before you left the chair, Mr. Speaker. I believe on the present resolution some members desire to make their addresses while you are still in the chair, and I would ask the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) to be good enough to make his statement before you leave the chair.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite prepared to make a short statement on the resolution at this time, but I should like to point out that there will be a number of occasions later when opportunities will be provided to speak on the measure. We propose to have it sent to the standing committee on marine and fisheries when it reaches second reading. There will be an opportunity to discuss the measure at length on other occasions. I would hardly believe that we would want to spend much time on the resolution stage, again on second reading, and again when we go into committee, and then have a further discussion in the standing committee on marine and fisheries. I will make my statement now. It will be a short one.
During the past two years we have considered the revision of the present fish inspection legislation. Fish inspection is carried on under two separate acts. Canned fish inspection is under the Meat and Canned Foods Act; other types of fish are inspected under the Fish Inspection Act. It is with the latter act that I am going to deal. This act was passed in 1914 to take care of the problem of pickled barrelled fish. Since then it has been amended on several occasions. We again reached the stage when we found we lacked the necessary statutory authority to meet present-day quality control problems. There was also the question of the validity of the act itself from a constitutional point of view.

Fish Inspection Act
Therefore the present act has been revised with three purposes in view: (1) to provide for inspection of fish which moves in interprovincial and export trade; (2) to revise the regulatory powers to meet present-day problems; and (3) to amplify and simplify some of the enforcement procedure.
The provisions of the existing Fish Inspection Act are not confined to export and interprovincial trade but deal with inspection generally. The act covers inspection of fish whether such fish is sold within the province or outside the province, and it is here the difficulty has arisen. Inspection, if it deals only with fish that is sold within a province, is a matter for provincial jurisdiction. Some years ago it was thought that this problem would be overcome by getting the provinces to pass enabling legislation, so-called legislation by adoption. Several of the provinces, where the act has been applied, passed acts which in effect said: "We adopt this act as our own, in so far as it might deal with matters which are outside dominion jurisdiction". Since 1932, however, there have been judicial decisions which cast a doubt on the legality of such an arrangement. So it was decided that one of the things that must be done to put our house in order so as tt>
be able to meet these problems was the revision of our basic inspection act.
Under the new act authority is sought for quality control and inspection of products which move in interprovincial and export trade. In connection with the revision of our legislation, we have had several conferences with provincial authorities, and before the revision was finally drawn up we had a conference with all the provinces. The officials of the fisheries divisions of the provincial governments agreed to co-operate with us and to recommend any necessary provincial legislation to cover any deficiency in respect of inspection, particularly at wholesale and retail levels, which is within provincial jurisdiction.
The second purpose, as mentioned before, was to extend the regulatory control under the act. Before regulations of any kind can ever be made the necessary statutory authority must exist. Parliament will be asked to pass an act giving the government the necessary power to meet the present-day quality control needs of industry. This does not mean that we are proposing at this stage any new regulations; we are merely seeking to establish the necessary statutory authority for instituting any inspection procedure whenever that becomes necessary. The industry will, [Mr. Mayhew.l
of course, be more interested in the inspection regulations themselves that might be proposed from time to time.
Again I call attention to the fact that we will be in a much better position to discuss this bill-and I hope we will confine ourselves to the bill-when we have it before us.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Dion in the chair.

Before making the few
remarks I intend to make on this matter, Mr. Chairman, and asking a couple of questions that worry me a little bit-I am sure they will not worry the minister-I want to take the opportunity of saying to the minister how greatly pleased we are with the cooperation he has given the fisheries board of Newfoundland and indeed how greatly the people of Newfoundland and the fisheries appreciate the work that has been done by him since he took over the office he now occupies.
I should like to remark, and I do not believe that it is hurting the feelings of anyone in this committee, that fish and fishery matters are of little concern to Canadians as a whole. This industry is more or less an orphan child of Canada, of interest to only a few of the provinces. I believe these provinces have been described as the "have not" provinces. I can assure hon. members that, with the entry of your newest province into confederation, you are likely to hear a great deal more about fish and fishery matters from this time on.
I am sure that if you will bear with me you will understand why you are likely to hear more about fish than you might be expecting to hear, because fish and Newfoundland have been more or less synonymous terms for a great number of years. In fact, I believe for practically four centuries Newfoundland's economy has been based on the fisheries and, to use a common term in Newfoundland, the fisheries are the backbone of the country. It was the fishery and all the business associated with the fishery that brought the settlers to Newfoundland, and it was the fishery that kept them there. When I speak of the fishery, I mean chiefly the cod fishery. As one of my friends boldly put it one day-and I certainly do not agree with him-it was a cod that brought people to Newfoundland, it was a cod that kept them there, and it was a cod that brought them to Canada. But I certainly do not agree with that remark in any way.
Up to 1894, practically ninety per cent of the export trade of Newfoundland was made up of fish and fishery products. That is not true today. The proportion now would be roughly as follows: wood products, approximately 48 per cent; mineral products, 26 per cent; and fishery products about 24 per cent. But that is not the true picture in any way, because the greater number of the population-that is of the wage-earning population-of the island of Newfoundland are
Fish Inspection Act
engaged in the fishery. The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay would be much more conversant with the picture than I am, but I should think 48 per cent to 49 per cent of those capable of working are engaged in the fishery. That is a fairly high figure. You can therefore appreciate the importance of this industry to Newfoundland as a whole.
As I said before, up to 1894, and in fact for many years after that, dried fish was the main industry. The changeover from dried fish to fresh frozen fish has taken place only in recent years; it started some ten or twelve years ago. I might give hon. members a little bit of local history.
In 1939 the commission of government of that time made a contract with General Seafoods Corporation of New York. As a term of that contract they agreed to build a plant in a place called Lapoile, Newfoundland, which is in the district represented by the deskmate of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay. The commission of government was to provide them with the sum of $200,000. They were to be given a monopoly for twenty-two years and they were to employ Newfoundland labour exclusively. The codfish fillets were to be imported into the United States free of duty. It was a beautiful proposition, as hon. members will readily realize, as far as we in Newfoundland were concerned. The only unfortunate thing that happened was that the fishing industry and those associated with it began lobbying. I believe the start of it was in Boston. The people there had powerful interests in Washington, and as a result the United States congress passed legislation which completely finished the proposition.
I mention this matter to the committee because Newfoundland fishing firms in the fresh fish industry are again faced with that same proposition. Only today I picked up a Newfoundland paper and on looking over the headlines I saw this one: "Newfoundland Fish Draw Protest". The subheading reads: "United States Fish Association Claims Imports Will Ruin United States Industry". As I say, this matter may not be relevant to the present discussion, but I cannot help bringing it to the attention of the minister because it has to do with his department. The chairman of the fisheries board made a statement on September 24 to this effect:
In regard to sales of frozen fish and herring to the United States market, the effect of devaluating the Canadian dollar in terms of the American dollar should be beneficial.
This particular statement, reported in the St. John's Evening Telegram, asks congress in Washington to make an investigation. Thomas D. Rice, executive secretary of the

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the committee will recall that prior to the war we had a large vote for the advertising of agricultural products. Much of that money was used overseas, and some of it used in Canada. During the war however there was no object in advertising overseas, because all the food was delivered to the British government, and it made distribution on a quota basis. There was no reason for advertising our food in Britain at that time. As a matter of fact during the greater part of the war, and for some little time thereafter, Britain did raise objection to the advertising of any particular food in that country, because they wanted to make distribution irrespective of where it came from.
Today however the position is somewhat changed, and we feel it is necessary and advisable to do more advertising than we have been doing. We have asked for an extra sum of money to be able to accomplish that. Speaking from memory, I think it will be found that when I get to the further supplementaries there will be still another amount to be added in order to take care of these advertising programs.
We are broadening out in order to advertise products in Canada. When it is reported that there is a surplus of a certain product we assist in advertising it in Canada in an effort to increase its consumption rather than to look entirely outside of Canada in order to find a market.

I am glad the minister has given that answer. I do not want to leave
Supply-Agriculture
the impression that I am opposed to advertising, because I think the department is wise to go ahead with this advertising program, especially of agricultural products that may be in surplus supply. Last year we had a surplus of honey, and I know the British Columbia people may have a surplus of apples. These advertising campaigns have certainly broadened the markets for various agricultural products.

What products are advertised in Great Britain? I know that people there have thought they were getting United States bacon when in fact they were getting our good Canadian bacon. We should advertise our bacon, our apples, our honey and other products. I know this is done at the different exhibitions held over there, but the fact remains that Canadian and United States bacon have got mixed up in the people's minds and I know that our western bacon is much superior to any such products coming into Great Britain today.

The position with regard to advertising in Great Britain is not too clear. We have been given to understand by those with whom we have come in contact that the British prefer that we do not advertise. I made that statement a year ago and to my surprise a question was asked in the British house, which I presume started from here, and the answer given was that they did not object. However, our experience is that they do object, no matter what the answer in the house may be.
I can quite understand why they should. The British are buying food from all over the world. All the food purchased is marketed by the government, not by individuals. If we went into Britain and advertised Canadian bacon as being the best in the world, if we tried to tell the people that that was what they ought to eat and thus induced the British consumer to demand that his government get Canadian bacon, I can understand the difficulty it would create for their government. It may be perfectly true that there is no law against it, that there is nothing to prevent its being done, but I have an idea that, if we did it, it would not be long before we ran into difficulties. For that reason we have thought it inadvisable to put on any definite program of advertising in Britain.
We do certain things when the opportunity presents itself. For example, the deputy minister came to me the other day and told me that we had not been allowing people to include butter in the parcels they were sending to Britain and he asked me what I thought about it. I told him that as some people thought we had a surplus of butter in Canada it might not be a bad thing to

Supply-Agriculture
allow people to put Canadian butter in their parcels instead of having Eaton's or Simpson's buy Danish butter to be sent over to Britain. Regulations are being sent out indicating that it will be quite proper to include Canadian butter in these parcels. This will be a form of advertising of Canadian butter. At some time we may have a surplus which we will want to sell and it might be a good thing to encourage people in this country to put it in their parcels so that our products would be advertised in an indirect way. Outside of that kind of action it is most difficult to evolve any plan to definitely advertise our products over there.
I hate to think I have been breaking the law in recent weeks by sending good Canadian butter to Britain. We have good products to sell and we should tell the world about them.
Has the trade been told that it is permitted to send Canadian butter to England? I have here a list of food that may be sent in parcels to England and butter is not included.

The decision was just made within the last seventy-two hours so I do not think there has been much opportunity for anyone to take advantage of it. I do not want it to be understood that the trade, as we understand that term, is to be permitted to do that sort of thing. I doubt very much if the trade would be permitted to do it, not because of anything we might do but because of what the British government might do if business people here were permitted to ship this particular product to their counterparts in Britain.
But there are companies like Eaton's and Simpson's and a few others that make a practice of putting up parcels to be sent to Britain by individuals in this country. Certain food products have been included in those parcels, but butter was not one of them. We are now saying that it is quite proper to put butter in. The reason it was not permitted to be put in last year was that we were bringing in butter from outside in order to supply our own people. Some people complained because some of the products being put in these parcels were Danish, but one could hardly complain about putting in food products from another country if we did not permit food products from this country to be included in the parcels. We now have sufficient butter to supply our own people and there is no reason why butter should not go into these parcels and serve as a form of advertising.

I remember the minister being somewhat critical about Canadians sending Darcels from Denmark to England, but the

only reason that was done was that you could not send butter from this country. The reason for that prohibition has been given by the minister.

I should like to ask a question in connection with a remark made by the minister the other evening, as reported on page 696 of Hansard, as follows:
If it has been fairly good, and if we want to market more products in the markets that are available, then I think we ought to produce them and put them on the market.
The question I intend to ask will apply equally to bacon, poultry and other products. Would it be possible to persuade the English to give us their quotas or commitments a year in advance of what they are doing now? It is practically impossible for a farmer to plan his poultry production unless he knows at least a year and a half in advance.

During the war we were able to make contracts that extended for more than twelve months; in some cases we were able to make contracts for two years, and in the case of wheat we were able to make a contract that extended for four years. On all other products two years was the limit. While we had those contracts it was possible to let the farmer know at least a year in advance what he was going to be required to supply under them. Unfortunately that is most difficult at the present time; in fact I think it is impossible. It is not because of anything we do about it. The British are battling in order to maintain their dollar position, and they come over here once a year and indicate to us how many dollars they have available to carry on trade with us. Then they try to divide those dollars among the different types of trade that we carry on with them. So much is allowed for agriculture.
After they have taken that position we have another discussion with them as to whether the amount can be increased in so far as our food products are concerned if more dollars are needed in order to take care of our surplus. What I was suggesting the other night was that, in our experience up to the present, we have not been able to supply as much as Great Britain finally agreed they had the dollars to buy of those products that we were discussing. As long as that is the position, I can only say to those who are saying that we have lost markets, or that we should be finding markets, that the only reason for finding more markets would be to produce more products. We are now consuming much more of all those products in Canada than we were prior to the war, and as to many of them even more than during the war. For that reason we have not so

much to export, but our difficulty up to the moment with the British has not been one of having been refused markets. We have found difficulty in supplying even those markets for which Great Britain has provided so many dollars to buy farm products.

I think the minister will agree with me that from the long term point of view, if we are going to continue to have markets in Great Britain for our agricultural products, we must be in a position to live up to the contracts into which we enter. We had a discussion on this matter a few nights ago when the minister's estimates were before the house previously, and he more or less pooh-poohed the idea that there was any chance we might lose markets in Great Britain because we had not lived up to our contracts. Nevertheless, from the long-range point of view, I still believe if we do not live rip to those contracts year after year there will be considerable disinclination on the part of the British to enter into further contracts with us with any idea, as far as they are concerned, that we will live up to them.
I should like to ask the minister what measures he thinks might be taken, and whether the government has any ideas in mind as to what steps we might take so that we would be in a position to meet our contracts. I refer particularly to bacon. Perhaps more than anything else we have been notably deficient in meeting our contracts for bacon. Then there are eggs in which we have also fallen down, and generally all agricultural products concerning which we enter into contracts to supply the British market.
Personally I think we are in a poor position to bargain with Great Britain or any other country if we are deficient in meeting the contracts into which we have entered. I would say that it places us in a bad bargaining position to have to go to a country and say: We contracted to supply you with 160 million pounds of bacon, and all we will be able to supply is 50 million pounds; we are sorry there is this big deficiency. It seems to me that our general agricultural policy should be directed along the line of securing sufficient supplies to meet our contracts. What particular steps may be necessary to do that is a pretty complicated matter, but nevertheless I do not like the idea of entering into contracts, which the minister said has been done year after year, to supply so many thousand pounds of this and so many tons of that, with the idea always in mind that we will not be able to live up to them.
I think that the minister should give us an explanation or a resume of what the government has in mind to meet the contracts which we have at the present time,
Supply-Agriculture
and the ones which we hope the minister will be able to enter into with Great Britain before the end of the year.

I have tried to tell the non. member on three or four occasions, and apparently I have not spoken plainly enough, that we do not intend to do any such thing. We have no intention of asking Canadian farmers to try to produce more bacon for the British at the present time. The chief reason for that is that the British have told us they have no dollars to pay for it. They have come over here for the last two years and have said: We would like your bacon all right; we could eat more of it but we have no dollars to pay you for it. Therefore they said that they did not want us to send it to them.
That is where we start from. Then we say to the British: Well, that may be all right, but we got into the habit of sending you a lot of bacon during the war, and our people still think that they should have the privilege of sending it to you if they have it. We say to the British that we would like them to sit down with us and estimate the greatest number of dollars that they can afford to pay for bacon. Then we say to them: We will try to bring down the quantity in the contract to the point where your dollars will pay for the bacon we do send. We understand one another. We know that they do not feel they are in a position to pay for any and so they say that they would just as soon we did not send it. They say: In order to keep some Canadian bacon on our market we are prepared to sign a contract that will cover a limited number of dollars We start off from there and we say to our farmers: Here is the contract price for bacon; that contract price will bring you a certain price for hogs. If you can sell your hogs for a better price somewhere else then do not worry about the British because after all they would just as soon you did not send them any.
That is what we are actually saying to the farmers today. What has been the result? During the last year somewhere between 50 and 70 per cent more pork has been consumed on the Canadian market than was consumed before the war. As a result of the fact that more is consumed on this market than before the war, hogs have been as much as 7 cents a pound dressed weight higher in Canada than you can get for them under the British contract. Why would any farmer insist on his hogs being sent to Great Britain at 7 cents a pound less than he can sell them for in Canada? He just is not going to do that. He will produce more hogs to sell in Canada at 7 cents a pound above

Supply-Agriculture
the British contract price than he would produce if you told him he had to sell them under the British contract at 7 cents a pound less.
I do not know any way to tell the farmer that he ought to have produced more hogs for Great Britain when he can get 7 cents a pound more by selling them in Canada. For that reason we have been saying that as long as the farmer can get that market at home we are not going to worry him about sending bacon to Great Britain, but we do say to the British that we would like them to continue the contract, that we would like them to undertake to take the maximum amount that we may have after we have sold all we can to the Canadian people so that when their difficulties are ended and they are able to provide the dollars we will still be in that market and they will know something about our product.
In that connection I have some figures which may be of interest, which I just happened to run across a few moments ago. They illustrate pretty well what is happening, and I only give them because they have some bearing on what we should be doing. I agree with the hon. member that it would be a good thing for the farmers of Canada if by some means or other they should come to the conclusion that they might produce more hogs than they are producing today, but at the same time I have no intention of going out and telling them so, or of trying to compel them, by means of legislation or regulation, to produce more hogs. I know how far I would get with that.
The point is that some farmers prefer to produce grain rather than hogs, and I do not blame them for that, either. A man can sow grain in the spring, let it grow and harvest it in the fall, and have considerable time to himself evenings and Sundays; and a farmer who can make enough money that way to live as he wants to live will not be easily induced to feed pigs and milk cows, which will keep him at home evenings and Sundays and all the rest of the time. So he decides to produce grain, and I would not quarrel with him over that. I know farmers too well to quarrel with them over such matters. They are going to make their own decisions, as they have always made them.
As a result we find that during the six months from January to June, 1948, the United Kingdom imported 35,000,000 pounds of bacon from Denmark, while for the same period in 1949 her imports from that country amounted to 58,000,000 pounds. In other words Great Britain obtained 15-8 per cent of her supplies in the first half of 1948 from Denmark, while she obtained 52-5 per cent of her supplies of bacon from that country [Mr. Gardiner.!	I
in the first six months of 1949. That means, for what it is worth, that Denmark is back to within two per cent of the position she occupied before the war in supplying the British market. It does not mean Denmark is supplying as much bacon as she supplied before the war; probably Britain is not eating as much. After all, bacon is the most expensive pork product you can eat, and when people are having difficulty in finding money they do not eat as much of the most expensive foods they can find. If you want to eat a really expensive product, eat bacon. Canada's position is that in the first six months of 1948 we supplied 167-5 million pounds of bacon to the British market, as compared with the figure of 35 million pounds from Denmark. For that period of time we supplied 74-8 per cent of all the bacon imported by Britain. In 1949, however, we supplied only 22-6 per cent as against Denmark's 52-5 per cent; that is, we supplied 25 million pounds as against 167 million pounds in the first six months of the previous year. One of the principal reasons for that change is that we are consuming more and more pork in Canada, at higher prices than the British are required to pay for the Wiltshire sides that enter into the production of bacon for that market.
I only give those figures to indicate that the trend is back toward the position we occupied before the war; and we are not trying to either induce or compel farmers to depart from their chosen practice. In my experience of almost fifteen years in this department I have found that 750,000 farmers all working on the job can make a better average decision about any of these matters than any member of this house, including the Minister of Agriculture. I do not intend to try to tell those 750,000 farmers what they should do. I try to give them the facts and let them form their own judgment, and that judgment is that they should not be producing as many hogs now as they did in the middle of the war.
I believe the pamphlet from which the minister was quoting figures a moment ago is the Searle Grain Company report of about two weeks ago?
No, that does not happen to be correct.
Is that not so?

If the figures are correct I imagine they would be the same no matter where they were found, but this happens to be a letter on Canadian livestock products, to foster a better meat industry, prepared by the industrial and development council of the meat packers.

In any event the figures are the same as those in this publication, and they are the figures which caused me to do a good deal of thinking, together with many other people who are engaged in the production of hogs. In his remarks the minister has left out of consideration altogether one thing about which he used to talk a good deal; that is, the long-term point of view as far as the hog industry of this country is concerned. Two or three years ago he would point out quite frequently that the future of the hog industry of Canada lay in the British market-
It does yet.

-and that we should bend every effort to retain that market. The minister just interjected, "It does yet", and with that remark I entirely agree. I think it does, and that if we are to have a healthy hog industry in this country we must have the British market for our surplus pork products, particularly our bacon. I think the minister will realize that is what I was getting at in what I said before he spoke; that in this country we should be following a policy which will enable us to supply the demand for bacon in Great Britain. It is quite true that at the present time Britain is short of dollars. However, she does have a certain amount of money, some of which she is still spending for bacon; and it seems to me that in order to ensure our market in future-and this is the very thing the minister used to emphasize so strongly only two years ago- everything possible should be done to meet the British demand for bacon. If the government can take any action to put us in a position to meet that demand, I think that action should be taken. In other words we should do our best to retain that market. I think it is very bad policy on our part, in spite of what the minister has said-and he really has not dealt with this point-to enter into contracts for a great deal more bacon or any other product than we can possibly supply.
I should like to put that in the form of a question. Whom does this fool? Since apparently it is not fooling the British people, the only conclusion I can reach is that it is designed to fool our own people, particularly our producers of hogs, when we enter into a contract, for 180 million pounds as we did last year, when from present indications we will not be able to supply more than 50 million pounds at the most. That sort of thing does not seem to be good business. Certainly it is not good business as far as our farmers are concerned.

Nor is it good business as far as our customers are concerned, or perhaps I should say our customer in Great Britain. The minister mentioned that the 750,000 farmers of this country are the people best equipped to decide what they should produce. With that statement I agree entirely. The point is, however, that they will produce those things on which they can make the greatest profit and at the same time have a reasonable assurance that their market will remain. They will not go into the production of hogs on a large scale and as a steady business, for example, if they believe the market for pork products is liable to disappear overnight, which is exactly what happened some two years ago. People sold off weaner pigs, feeder pigs, brood sows and everything else because they were afraid of what was going to happen to the hog market.
Then we had 48 per cent more delivered than before. Some of my friends were saying they had sold them off.

No. All you have got to do is look at the figures. You know it as well as I do. You have a great deal less delivered now than you had in 1947, which is the year I am speaking of. The general reason that farmers will grow hogs or will not grow hogs is, as the minister knows, the hog-barley ratio or the relationship between the amount of feed grains available and the price of those in relation to the price of hogs. During the past year the people who have been producing hogs have had a certainty that, as far as we are concerned in Alberta, the price of select hogs would not fall below $27.15 a hundred, dressed weight. That was the basic price. On that basis they were able to make their plans and go ahead.
At the present time quite a number of people I know are more than a little bit nervous as to what the situation is likely to be after the first of the year. They know that until the first of the year that is the least price they can receive; they can feed their hogs on that basis and more or less make their plans accordingly. But with the devaluation of the pound, and the fact that we have not been able to anything like meet the British contract, and the general uncertainty in their minds as to what the situation may be with regard to the marketing of pork after the first of the year-I think the minister knows I am not putting this argument up for political or any similar reasons; and he knows this as well as I do-there is a considerable amount of perturbation among the hog raisers as to what their situation is going to be after the first of the coming year. A few nights ago I asked the minister if he could give any assurance to these people, or

Supply-Agriculture
if he could assure them in any way. He gave a long answer and, I am sorry to say, an evasive one. It was not one that was of any use to the ordinary farmer who is producing hogs. So I would ask the minister again if he can give any information, which would be of value to the hog producers of this country as a whole, as to what their position is likely to be after the end of this year.

In the years since the beginning of the war, I have followed the practice of letting the opposition do the prophesying as to what is going to happen; as a result I have found that they were usually wrong. I am therefore not going to start to prophesy now.
I did not ask for a prophecy.

You asked me what is going to happen next year. That is a prophecy.
The position in relation to hogs in 1947, which was referred to a few moments ago, is that every member who spoke on the opposition side of the house-and it did not matter from what section of the opposition he spoke-told the story about killing little pigs and marketing sows. That was in the fall of 1947. In the first six months of 1948 more hogs were marketed in good A and B grades than were marketed in the first six months of 1947.
No.
And there were 48 per cent more marketed-
Have you any figures to support that statement?
Yes, the figures are on the record
I think you will find you are wrong.

There were 48 per cent more hogs marketed in January, 1948, to provide Wiltshire sides, than were marketed in January of the previous year. It is true that after October of 1948 the production of hogs dropped. That was all foretold by the officials of the statistics department. That was all foretold when we were discussing the question in 1947. If it is of any interest to my hon. friend, the present position is that the production is going in the opposite direction. Production was dropping in the latter part of 1948 and all through the early part of 1949. The production is now going up and we are having more and more hogs coming to market in addition to the number that came last year. That fact indicates to me that these 750,000 farmers, or that proportion of them that produces hogs, have an idea that

maybe they are going to get a little better return for their hogs in the months that lie ahead.
The hog-barley ratio is better, is it not?

The hog-barley ratio at the present moment is not too good. But at the same time, if you want to take the same document from which my hon. friend usually quotes his figures, it will be found that, if you can get $30 a hundred for dressed hogs, you can get $2.16 a bushel for your barley. That is considerably more than barley is selling for, and hogs are still selling around 33 cents.
No, they are not. They are $29.50 in Calgary.
I am speaking of one place all the time, not Calgary; I am speaking of one of the central points of Canada.
At Toronto they are $29.50 in today's market, or according to this morning's paper.
They may be $29.50 tonight. But these figures bring you down to the end of August.
That is not present prices.

That is about as near up to the present as you can get reliable figures for. The fact that hogs were quoted on the Toronto market at 29 cents yesterday does not mean that they were not quoted a week ago at over 30 cents; and it does not mean that they may not be quoted before the end of next week at 27 cents. But the average over the week may amount to figures similar to those which were obtained in the latter part of August. As a matter of fact, you cannot go on the daily returns in connection with these prices. Let us go back to the point that my friend is arguing, that you do not get enough for your barley.
No, I was not.
That is what the ratio between the price of hogs and the price of barley means, that if it gets down to a certain level, you are not getting enough.
Do not try to put words into my mouth. I was not arguing that for a moment.
Order.

If you can produce 100 pounds of pork by feeding 500 pounds of feed, you can get $2.16 a bushel for your barley if you get 30 cents for your hogs. If you get even 20 cents for your hogs you can still get $1.44 for your barley, which is

just about the price that barley is. In other words, the price of hogs is 50 per cent higher than the figure which is necessary in order to produce the price of barley.
Excuse me, but may I ask a question?
You have asked a number, and I am trying to answer some of them.
I take it that this does not take into consideration the other costs of [DOT] feeding hogs. This is simply the price of barley. It has nothing to do with the labour involved and the land.

My hon. friend feeds hogs.
I should like to ask him if he cannot buy barley, feed it to the hogs, and make money.
I would not be in the business if I could not.
Of course you would not. And the farmer can make more money when he grows his own grain and feeds his own hogs than you can make buying your hogs and buying your barley.
I am growing barley.

So the argument still is that the farmer is not doing too badly. If he can produce the 100 pounds-and if he is a good feeder he can do so-by feeding 400 pounds of feed, then he gets $2.70 for his barley, at 30 cents for the pork; and at 20 cents for the pork he gets $1.80. People talk about not getting enough for their wheat when they get $2 a bushel. If he is a good hog feeder he can get $3.37 for his wheat by feeding it to hogs.
If he can make 100 pounds with 350 pounds of feed. Look at your figures.
No; if he can make 100 pounds of pork on 400 pounds of feed. I am sure my hon. friend will agree that he himself is a good enough feeder to be able to do that.
I think you will find that the figure is 350.

No; the one I have just quoted is 400. The 350 is $2.88-no, it is not even down to 350. It is 375. There is no 350 in the table. At 450 he can get $2.40 and so on. The table indicates that it is not the case of the farmer not being able to make enough feeding the hogs that has caused him to come down in production. It is something else, and I am not going to try to guess what that is. It is a different thing with different farmers. I know what it would be in my case if I had to feed the pigs myself and clean up the pigpens. You can be sure that

as long as I could get the price that I can get for grain now I probably would not do the job. That is one of the reasons why many of them take that position. They say, "We would rather have the returns that we get from the grain and not have to employ anyone since we do not want to do it ourselves. We do not want to have to employ labour in order to get the job done." I am not going to try to give all the reasons, but there are many. They are not doing it; that is the main thing.

With respect to the marketing of fruit and vegetables, the minister's department maintains inspection services across Canada. I understand that a corps of these inspectors is employed more or less on a permanent basis, but the greater number are temporary employees employed during the period of shipping fruit or vegetables. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that -while in British Columbia these inspectors have done a fair and reasonable job, in view of the importance of the inspectors' position between the producers and the consumers, has the minister given consideration to having the greater number of these inspectors termed "permanent employees"? I do not think one can expect a man to take up inspection work as a career if he is employed for five or six months a year and takes it as a part-time job.
Has the minister given consideration to the training of these inspectors? It is a very important matter so far as the industry in British Columbia is concerned. No doubt the minister knows that the industry maintains, at its own expense, a competent staff of inspectors who are of great assistance in British Columbia. At this time I want to express the appreciation of the industry for what the senior officials are trying to do in British Columbia with a very limited and part-time staff.
The minister may say that there is not enough for them to do the year round, but I just want to bring this to his attention. Just the other evening, my colleague, the hon. member for Yale, and I were walking down one of the streets of Ottawa looking into shop windows. There we saw four or five boxes of scrubby Ontario apples, I presume, piled into our extra fancy boxes from British Columbia. I presume the apples were being sold as jumbo pack apples. They were obviously all culls. They were being displayed in a large store window in our boxes labelled "extra fancy O.K. brand." Anybody knows if you buy an apple from an O.K. box that apple is O.K. Has the minister given consideration to increasing the number of permanent employees and increasing their salaries? When one considers the importance of these men of the inspection

Supply-Agriculture
service to the industry, to the producers and to the consumers, and compares the salaries received by other very much less important people, he will agree that these men are entitled to receive treatment that would cause them to consider the inspection of fruit and vegetables as a career which would enable them to give the best service possible to this important industry.

As the hon. member has pointed out, the grading of apples in British Columbia is done at least as well as it is done in any part of Canada. The actual grading of the apples is done by men and women employed by the trade or by the producers. In their plants they have certain machines to grade apples with regard to size. I have watched them at work. They have individuals standing alongside the machines picking them out, and when the job is done it is presumed that one of the best grading jobs is done in Canada.
Right.

All our inspectors have to do is to go along and look at them and come to the conclusion that the job is well done. When they have done that they have done their job. It takes a certain number of them but it does not take nearly as many inspectors to take care of a job of that kind at any other time of the year as it does when the apples are being shipped and marketed. I presume when we hire part-time men-the hon. member will know more about this than I do-we hire men who have been pretty well trained in the business themselves. I would imagine that when they go out to pick up men to do this job they may take some fellow who has some time on his hands at that time of the year and who has had experience in doing the job. They put him on for a few weeks or a few months. It is the same principle that is followed all the way through our agricultural activities. We do the same thing with P.F.R.A. and with P.F.A.A. It would be impossible to employ as many men and women for the whole year as are needed to do the job at that time of the year. But I do agree with the suggestion that we ought to get our staffs of competent persons who are employed for the full time up to a number which will see to it that the job is done as it ought to be done. If it can be shown by anyone that that is not so at the present time I am quite sure the department would be open to consider any representations made.

Can the Minister of Agriculture say what the attitude of his department is toward the proposal which I understand was made by the food and agriculture organization that a food pool be set up and that food
[Mr. Herridge.J
be sold from that pool to European nations and paid for in their own currencies where they lack dollars? I understand a similar proposal was made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I should say that it actually originated with the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I think the minister will agree that a proposal of that kind would help greatly toward the stabilizing of maximum production and sales to Europe.

In answer to the question I can only say that I am on record in connection with the matter. The question was discussed at Quebec when the FAO was set up, and it was discussed again in Copenhagen and in Geneva. I was present on all three occasions and expressed my views with regard to it, and they were in agreement with those which had been presented to those organizations by Sir John Orr, who was then president of the FAO. I do not know of anything that was more completely earned than the Nobel prize which was presented to Sir John Orr during this present week for the, I would say, noble job that he has done in connection with the whole matter.
Shame!
You can do better than that.

The difficulty in connection with it is that there are too many people in the world who still think dollars mean more than anything else. The only reason I have heard presented by anybody as to why a food pool should not be provided in order to see that all people are properly fed throughout the world and producers able properly to market their products is that it might cost somebody too much. I do not agree that it would cost anyone too much. For example, this country carried 600,000,000 bushels of wheat through a very considerable part of the war, and no part of its population had anything to do with financing it, except some 200,000 farmers who produced that wheat. They carried 600,000,000 bushels of wheat to have it there towards the end of the war to feed the people in Europe who otherwise would have starved.
If 200,000 farmers can do that, then I do not know what good argument there is to come from any of the great nations of Europe as to why they should not see to it that surpluses are carried out of years of very high production into years of very low production, and particularly in connection with commodities such as wheat. I am all for it, but I do not know that I could carry all the people of Canada with me.
I wonder if the minister would go a step further and say that the dominion government is in favour of it?
The government of Canada let me make three speeches on it, and did not kick me out.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak on this item because it affects the constituency of Regina City, which I have the honour to represent in this House of Commons. Before I proceed further I think it would be well for me to say a few words on the history of the location of that city, and something concerning its development, so that hon. members in the house may appreciate some of the difficulties we have with water in that area, and so that they may understand, as the successors of former parliamentarians, they have inherited certain responsibilities.
When the Canadian Pacific Railway was built into western Canada it was understood that it was to pass along the north side of the Qu'Appelle lakes, and that Regina city was to be located in the Qu'Appelle valley. There, in that broad valley, was an abundant supply of water, shelter from the winds, a spot of great natural beauty, an ideal location for any city.
The railway was to extend farther west along the Qu'Appelle valley and along the Saskatchewan river to Estuary and along the Red Deer, and then the Bow river to Calgary. I am quite sure that the parliament of that day took the advice of the people of western Canada who knew something of the country, and agreed to build the railway in close proximity to surface water, so that the settlements which were bound to take place along the right-of-way would have no water problems.
What happened? The survey party of the Canadian Pacific Railway met with some right-of-way difficulties at Fort Qu'Appelle. It withdrew and ran the survey across .the prairies thirty to sixty miles to the south of this natural water supply, across the dry plains. They ran it from Brandon to Medicine

Supply-Agriculture
Hat. As a result we have Regina, Moose Jaw, Swift Current, Gull Lake, and many other small towns and villages in perpetual water difficulty.
I wish to deal more particularly with Regina. They located Regina on the old pile of bones or Wascana creek. It was there the Indians met after they slaughtered buffalo, jerked the meat and made pemican-there was enough water for that, but very little more. Since that time the city has developed tremendously and met with many adversities, one of which was the cyclone of 1912 which left a path of death and destruction through the city.
There was the drought period of the thirties. More recently, last winter, there was a disastrous fire which wiped out the barns and rolling stock of the transportation system. It has faced all these difficulties, and met them. It has faced all its problems and settled them-and it has always had very serious problems. One of the most serious has been the problem of the shortage of water.
To understand that problem I believe the committee should know something of the geology of the country. In the ice age the great ice cap lay over Labrador. The glacier flowed across Hudson bay and down across the prairies toward the gulf of Mexico. As the ice receded it left deposits of glacial drift -that is, gravel and boulders. At different places on the prairies there is evidence of this, and here we find water. As the glacier receded a great lake formed over that prairie country into which rivers flowed. Silt was deposited to a depth, at Regina, of 42 feet. It is impervious to water. At places the glacial drift comes to the surface, but it is difficult to ascertain the extent of this or the amount of water it contains without drilling -and drilling is a costly business.
We drill wells to depths of 50, 100 and 200 feet in order to obtain variable supplies of water. We have had the opinion of some of the greatest water engineers on the continent, such as Mr. N. S. Hill, Jr., of New York; R. O. Wynne-Roberts of Toronto; H. E. Simpson of the university of North Dakota and Professor Forsberg of the university of Saskatchewan. Their opinions vary slightly but they all state that in this glacial drift there is a limited supply of water and that we are now drawing beyond the limit of safety.
Last spring we seeded our gardens and planted our flowers. Our flowers came up, our gardens grew as they do there in the early spring when you have moisture; the flowers came into blossom and our lawns were green. Then came the hot weather and our gardens and flowers dried up and our lawns

became brown. One hot day in the summer when it was 105 in the shade we could get no water on the second stories of our homes.
This is a serious problem. In order to obtain water we must go to Buffalo Pound lake, which lies in the Qu'Appelle valley about 45 miles northwest of Regina. Buffalo Pound lake is formed by the runoff water of the great plain and is deepened by a dam thrown across the valley. Normally the water from the runoff down the Qu'Appelle valley is used to irrigate 30,000 to 40,000 acres of hay lands where they have a method of flood irrigation. Then farther down they carry on market gardening.
An urban municipality has priority over a rural municipality and irrigated land in order to obtain water for its population. When we take water from Buffalo Pound lake we will jeopardize the supply of water for those who live below. I should like to ask the minister if there is sufficient money in the estimates to provide for a project to maintain the water level in Buffalo Pound lake. This would have to be done by pumping water from the Saskatchewan river. When the dam is built at Elbow the water will flow by gravity down the Qu'Appelle valley and there will be no problem, but in the intervening years something must be done to protect these people who grow hay, who have market gardens, or who have summer cottages along the valley right down to Brandon and Winnipeg.

I want to say to the Minister of Agriculture that I am happy that an agreement has been reached between the government and the Canada Land and Irrigation Company. It is now up to the government to carry on an extension of that program. As far as my speech during the throne speech debate is concerned, and perhaps I should not refer to it, may I say that the argument was not between the minister and myself, it was between certain newspapers out west and myself. I should like to refer to a report that appeared in one of those papers. When I asked a question the other day the Minister of Agriculture gave me a rather smart answer which was applauded by many Liberal members.
It was an answer to a smart question.

The minister said that he did not publish either paper. I knew, and I am sure that most hon. members knew, that the minister did not publish either paper, but most hon. members do not realize the statement that appeared in the press that day. I am going to read the report that appeared in one of the papers. When the government goes into business I think this house should

be the first to be informed and not the defeated Liberal candidate in any particular constituency. That is what happened in this connection and that is why I refer to it. The Medicine Hat News of Thursday, September 29, contained the following report on the front page-
What year?

1949. The report reads: Government Buys Canada Land
The Canadian cabinet this morning accepted the Canada Land and Irrigation Company deal. This means the government buys the company's assets on the Bow river extension, including the Ronalane-Redcliff project, for a sum of $2,250,000.
An expenditure of $3,500,000 in addition will be required to complete all extension works to bring the water to Medicine Hat. In addition the Alberta government has a stake of $1,250,000 in the development.
The announcement was officially made to the News this afternoon by Harry Veiner, of Brooks, Liberal candidate in the last general election, after a long distance telephone communication from agricultural minister James G. Gardiner.
Mr. Gardiner stated that the company's offer to sell had been accepted by the cabinet this morning and would be announced in the house later today. Confirmation will be forwarded to Dave W. Hays, local manager of Canada Land. It consummates a proposal originated some months before the election in a conference between the three principals mentioned above, and brings closer to realization a thirty-five year dream of Medicine Hat residents.
If, as the minister tells us, this deal has gone through, I am glad and I am sure every voter and resident in the Medicine Hat area and the drought area of that part of the province is happy about it. But this will depend upon whether the government carries on with that project and shows that it means business. We have wasted another year. Nothing has been done to enlarge the canal or to extend the project further. We do not expect that anything will be done before next year, but I can assure you that we do expect to see some action taken in connection with this project.
When this project is completed I think the citizens in the semi-arid areas surrounding Medicine Hat should be given the opportunity to settle on irrigated land. When the Rolling Hills area was settled not so many years ago, shortly after the drought years of 1935, 1936 and 1937, not one farmer in the Medicine Hat area was given an opportunity to move to that irrigated area. They were all brought in from Saskatchewan. We have no particular objection to bringing people in from Saskatchewan but we want to give our own farmers, who have experienced drought for twenty-five years, an opportunity to settle on some of that land. I hope that the dominion government will take that into consideration in the settlement of the land and give some of our dry-land farmers an opportunity to settle on that project. My hon. friend says
Supply-Agriculture
that they may bring all Liberals in there to defeat me, but I may say that if they thought they were bringing all Liberals into the Rolling Hills area they were badly fooled because first of all they voted C.C.F. and now they are mostly Social Crediters.
They are getting crazier every day.
They are advancing. They will get along.

I am sure that once they are Social Crediters they will always be Social Crediters. I had a question to ask on item No. 30, but it went by so fast that I missed it. I presume, however, I can ask it now on the item we are dealing with at the present time. It is in connection with the Ross creek irrigation project. No doubt the minister is acquainted with that. There are about eight or ten miles of canal built under the P.F.R.A. What I should like to know is the amount that has been spent on the canal up to the present time, and also if it is the intention of the P.F.R.A. to complete the canal up to the distribution point, and also the gates of the dam. I should like to know if it is the intention of the government to finish the project this fall.

As to the questions that were just asked, in the first place it is not the responsibility of the federal government to carry out any irrigation projects in Alberta. It is the responsibility of the government of Alberta, and it is the responsibility of the provincial governments in other provinces, to carry out irrigation work. The land that the federal government purchased from the Canada Land and Irrigation Company was purchased for the purpose of carrying out a program which was announced in 1936, and which has been carried on steadily from 1936 down to the present time. It is a policy of resettling the lands in the dry areas of western Canada.
It was stated a few moments ago by the hon. member for Medicine Hat that we put in the Rolling Hills project before the war, and we did, but it was stated at the same time that provision was not made for taking local people onto that project. One person out of every three is a local person. We took two from outside for every one who was taken from the area immediately surrounding the Rolling Hills project. It may be argued that we should have taken two from the local district for every one we took from elsewhere, but after all most of the people who were living in that district were already on irrigated land. We followed the practice for one-third of the area of attempting to take the sons of some of those who did not have

Supply-Agriculture
sufficient land, and we brought in people from dry areas in the neighbourhood in order to take up the other two-thirds. All of them, of course, were from one or another of-the western provinces.
This particular project is somewhat similar to that but on a larger scale. The land itself, which is being utilized for the purpose, will belong to the federal government. It will be utilized for the purpose of making it possible to move people off submarginal lands where we are now paying considerable sums through prairie farm assistance in order to maintain them in submarginal areas. As many of those people as can be will be moved onto these areas that will be supplied with water.
It is true that east of the area we have purchased there are somewhere in the neighbourhood of 70,000 acres of land upon which water can be placed, and to the west there is also about 70,000 acres of land, in round figures, that can be brought under irrigation, but all of those lands belong to the provincial government. They are actually the property of the provincial government, and they became the property of the provincial government when natural resources were returned to the provinces in 1931. I repeat that, in so far as there being any responsibility on any particular government to do anything about those lands, the responsibility is on the provincial government and not on the federal government.
It is true, however, that there have been discussions with regard to the provision of water for the lands both west and east of the Canada Land and Irrigation Company properties which we have purchased. There have been discussions as to ways and means of putting water on these other lands. The federal government is prepared to sit down and discuss with the provincial government ways and means of having that done. As to the amount of money which has been provided for the purpose in previous estimates, the intention was to spend a certain sum of money, something over $2 million, in the development of the ditches that have already been put in by the Canada Land and Irrigation Company for the purpose of making it possible to carry sufficient water in those ditches to supply the lands which can be irrigated to the west, and which in all probability will be developed by the province when they are developed, and to supply water for the lands to the east.
In other words, the water will have to be carried 198 miles to be exact. I was going to say 200 miles, and possibly you might remember that figure longer. The water has to be carried in the neighbourhood of 200 miles from the Bow river down beyond Calgary. Persons who drive west to Calgary on
IMr. Gardiner.]
No. 1 highway travel around a little lake called McGregor lake just before they reach Calgary. That is the first storage east of Calgary having to do with that system. The ditches extend farther on, having been put there originally by the Canada Land and Irrigation Company, almost to the Saskatchewan boundary north of Medicine Hat, but those ditches east of the Vauxhall project have not been utilized to any great extent for supplying water and have remained in disuse from the time when they were first constructed in the early part of the century. It is intended to develop those projects further or at least to enter into arrangements with the provincial government under which we may give some assistance towards the development of them, but not because it is our responsibility.
It is because we realize that the costs in connection with projects of this kind are considerable, that probably some benefits will accrue to all the people of Canada because of their development, and for that reason probably we should give some assistance. I do not want the committee, or the hon. member for Medicine Hat, to go away with the idea that there is any direct responsibility, constitutional or otherwise, on this government to do that job. As long as any government, whether it be that of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba or any other province, approaches the problem by trying to convince everyone that this is a federal job, all I can say is that they are approaching it from an entirely wrong point of view. The federal government has spent nearly all the money that has been spent by any government upon these projects. Certainly practically all the money that has been spent since the present Alberta government took over the administration of that province has been spent by the dominion. I do not intend to accept the suggestion from any member of this house or any member of the government of Alberta that this government has not been meeting all its obligations. It has been going away beyond its obligations and spending millions of dollars in order to make it possible for people out in Alberta to have irrigation.
We are quite prepared to sit down and discuss the question further, but there is one thing I am going to say very plainly. We are not going to sign every document any member of the government of Alberta wants to draw up, call an agreement, sign and send down here to us. We do not intend to do that. Those are the only kind of documents before the people of Alberta or before this government at the present time. There are no agreements before this government, though we have indicated our desire and

7G5
intention to sit down and discuss this matter at any time with the government of that province, and as far as I know the government of Alberta is prepared to sit down and discuss it with us. But when someone like the hon. member for Medicine Hat gets up during an election and makes the kind of speeches he made, indicating to the people that because for the last twenty years federal governments had done nothing, the present government was not going to do anything, and that all this talk about buying Canada Land and Irrigation was only so much hot air for consumption during election time-
On a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I am going to ask the minister to withdraw that statement.
I am not going to.
That is one statement I have never made, that it was nothing but hot air.

The statement you made meant that, even if you did not say it. I have your own advertisement here, signed by yourself, and I could produce two or three more. This is by no means the worst of them, but I am going to be more than fair and read one of the milder ones.
I don't own that paper.

No, but you paid for this advertisement; you published it. Here is what it says:
As thousands of electors in this district will not be able to get into the big tent, they are interested in the answers to the following questions.
Is that the circus tent?
That is the circus tent that you prepared for the people of Medicine Hat in order to induce them not to vote Liberal.

What amount has been paid to the Canada Land and Irrigation Company for their interest in the irrigation scheme known as the Redcliff-Ronalane?
When that advertisement was published my hon. friend knew no one had ever said that any money had been paid the Canada Land and Irrigation Company.
May I ask the minister what is the date of that?

It is the date you paid to put it in the Medicine Hat News, in June, 1949. At the bottom it says:
Inserted by the Medicine Hat federal constituency social credit association. Keep in step with Alberta! Vote social credit. Wylie.
Supply-Agriculture Mr. Harkness: And they did.

Then it goes on to say:
When will the actual construction work start?
Who has the contract for the actual work?
We should have asked the Liberal candidate; he was probably the only one who knew.

And it goes on:
How does the dominion Liberal government expect to socialize farming within the boundaries of this an autonomous province?
In other words he did not believe we were ever going to purchase the land and do anything at all about putting farmers upon it.
Why haven't you signed the agreement between the Canada Land and the Alberta government as you had promised to sign?
Then he goes on with this:
The people want the answers to these questions. Promises of irrigation are strictly out in this district. Keep in step with Alberta. Vote social credit. Wylie.
I say this is one of the milder advertisements. There were a number of others along slightly different lines, insinuating all the way through that this job was not going to be done. Only a few nights ago in this very chamber the hon. member made another speech of the same sort in which he insinuated that there was not much likelihood of this contract ever being carried out. It is all very well for him to say he was reading from the press. If I read everything the press has had to say about me, we would be here until next year. These things that appear in the press are the opinions of those who write them; and the only report that went out to Medicine Hat on the day indicated, no matter what the press had to say, was a report direct to the company that we were prepared to continue negotiations for the purchase of the property. Those negotiations have continued from that day until today, when it was finally agreed that the contract could be signed.
I do not want to be misunderstood, or to have someone say in the Medicine Hat News that the contract has been signed. I am telling hon. members, as I did a few moments ago, that the contract cannot be signed until we have completed our negotiations not only with the individual representing the company here but with the company itself, whose headquarters are located in London, England. Those negotiations are going on, and we have every reason to believe that they will be concluded successfully, that the contract will be signed, that the money will be paid and that we will proceed with the development of that project on that basis. But I want it clearly understood not only by the hon. member for Medicine Hat but by all others that the initial responsibility for this sort of thing

Supply-Agriculture
does not rest with this government. It rests with the government of Alberta; and it is only because we are interested in resettling an area which was originally settled by the dominion government when the natural resources were under the control of the federal authorities that this government has asked the people of Canada to take an interest in the matter. Up to the present time they have taken an interest to the extent of well over $30 million, and in these estimates we are asking hon. members to vote $7,500,000 for these larger projects and $3 million for P.F.R.A. In other words this year we are asking for $10,500,000, which is just about one-third of the total amount that has been spent since 1936 in carrying on all these P.F.R.A. activities throughout the three prairie provinces. As soon as the estimates are through the house we are prepared to sit down with the government of Alberta and discuss what they think ought to be assumed by the federal government. At the same time we shall feel quite free to suggest what we think they should assume in order to get these projects under way. I am quite sure that when we do get together we will be able to reach satisfactory conclusions, providing the hon. member for Medicine Hat does not make too many speeches.
I have no intention of carrying on a verbal battle with the Minister of Agriculture.
What are you doing?

What are you doing sitting over there? May I say this. In fairness, I think the minister should read some of the advertisements which were put in the paper by the Liberal candidate in the constituency and which precipitated these questions. If those were read, I think hon. members would understand why these questions were asked. When you have someone going around the constituency saying that the deal is all through-and the same thing appeared on the 29th of last month-something which is not true according to the minister's own words in a telephone communication with the defeated Liberal candidate, then I think it is time that something was done.
I have no intention of holding up any of the irrigation works. I believe that we should do everything possible to complete every project. I do not entirely blame the provincial government of any province, as the minister does. I have listened to campaign speeches in Saskatchewan where they have accepted the responsibility of getting some of these projects. I have heard what they are going to do with that dam across the Saskatchewan river. They have told us about that. I am sure that some of my 
C.C.F. friends can back me up on that. I think it is fairly well understood that, with respect to that irrigation project mentioned in the Meek report, the main responsibility falls on the dominion government. I think that was fairly well understood in that report.
That is not in the report.

It is in the report, and I think it is fairly well understood that the main responsibility falls upon the dominion government. No matter what the Minister of Agriculture says about the government of Alberta, I may say this in connection with the Canada Land and Irrigation Company. The dominion government had their experts; the Canada Land and Irrigation Company had their manager, Dave W. Hays; and the provincial government had some men on it. They investigated the whole situation and they agreed as to the amount each would carry. The provincial government signed that agreement and sent it down to Ottawa for the signature of the dominion government. We are still waiting for that. Now that the project is taken over by the dominion government, there is no need to sign that tripartite agreement. But may I ask the minister this question. When the dominion government bought out the Canada Land and Irrigation Company, did they consult the provincial government?
Yes.
Did the provincial government agree?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Next question.

The minister says that the provincial government did agree to the purchase of this company by the dominion government. According to the minister's statement, and according to some press reports from Ottawa, the provincial government had about $1,500,000 ready to put into the purchase of the agreement.
No, they did not.
I am going to read you the press report. You do not have to take my word for it.
You can get into difficulties when you go to the press too much.

I may be getting into difficulty but I am sure I am not in the difficulty that the minister is in. At no time did the provincial government say that they would assist in the purchase of the Canada Land and Irrigation Company?
No, not to us.
I doubt very much if the provincial government ever agreed, or ever said to the Minister of Agriculture that they would like to see the dominion government take over that project.

Does my hon. friend doubt my word? Is that what he is saying? Is he saying that he thinks I am lying about it? I went to Edmonton prior to getting the firm offer from the Canada Land and Irrigation Company. I met four of the members of the government, including the premier, in the premier's office. One of the gentlemen sitting here at the table in front of me was with me at the time. I presented the whole project to them, just as it has been carried through. They agreed that it was the best possible thing to do; and as a matter of fact there are letters on file to the same effect. There is not any question about that at all. It was agreed to by the provincial government when four members of the government were present.

I must say a word on this matter. Some people may be facetious about the south Saskatchewan irrigation project if they want to be, but the fact remains that the constituency in which I live happens to be in the dust bowl; and I can tell hon. members that drought conditions this year again are serious, as the hon. member for Regina City pointed out. At one time this year you could go out in an automobile on a highway and not be able to see the front of the engine because the dust was blowing so badly. You could go out on the golf course and try to putt your ball into the hole on a green but there were so many grasshoppers in the way that it would not go straight.
Do you blame the Minister of Agriculture for that?

The situation is serious. I am amazed to hear the Minister of Agriculture tonight get up and state that irrigation is not the responsibility of the federal government

and that is what he said, if I understood him correctly-because for forty years the Liberal party has been promising at every federal election and every provincial election that they were going to take effective action on irrigation. I remember what happened back in 1940. We have a little creek in the town of Moose Jaw not far from the main street. I remember the Liberal candidate getting up to speak, and from the way he talked I thought ships would be sailing down that Moose Jaw creek from Hudson bay. In 1945 I remember the minister and his party made a specific promise about the south Saskatchewan irrigation project. I have quoted it before in the house, and I am going
